subtitle: Star Citizen's technical model, GTA's climb, Hearts of Iron at the corporate scale. Information is the scarce commodity and attention is the one you cannot buy.

milestones.title: Prototype spike (delivered)
milestones.goal: Answer the two questions that could have killed the project: can a deterministic belief simulation be made legible, and can one engineer render a real-scale planet you fly to and from without a loading screen.
milestones.gate: Both answered yes. out/world-dump.txt traces a corporate collapse back four causes and shows two NPCs disagreeing for legible reasons; the client flies orbit to ground to orbit continuously, with water, weather and a town.

milestones.title: Architecture and the split
milestones.goal: Turn the spike into a structure before building anything complex on it. Cargo workspace, Unreal modules, the god-files split along real seams, and a build that refuses to compile a layering violation.
milestones.gate: No source file over 500 lines; every UE module declares three or fewer dependencies except LedgerGame; adding an illegal dependency fails CI with a named rule; the scripted flight renders identically to before the split.

milestones.title: Terrain to production standard
milestones.goal: The terrain stops being a spike. Stable LOD with no popping, collision wherever a body can be, caves and overhangs, biome-driven material blending, and a streaming budget that holds at speed.
milestones.gate: Fly a 200 km transect at 300 m and at 900 m/s: no holes, no popping that reads as a seam, no frame over 16 ms, and collision present under the ship at every point along it.

milestones.title: Planetary bodies and orbital mechanics
milestones.goal: A solar system that moves. Planets, moons, rings and stations on real orbits, axial tilt, rotation, day and night, seasons, eclipses — all deterministic from seed and all consistent between the map and the sky.
milestones.gate: Stand on a surface and watch a moon rise, transit and set on the schedule the orbital model predicts. Fly to it. The ephemeris and the sky agree to the arcminute.

milestones.title: Atmosphere, weather and environment
milestones.goal: Air that behaves. Layered atmospheres per body, volumetric weather that moves and matters, storms with real wind fields, temperature and pressure as physical quantities the rest of the game reads.
milestones.gate: Fly into a storm front: visibility, wind loading on the ship and cockpit audio all change together, and the same storm is visible from orbit in the place the weather model puts it.

milestones.title: Ship framework: hulls, components, subsystems
milestones.goal: Ships as systems, not props. A component graph — power plant, thrusters, fuel, cooling, avionics, life support, shields — with real dependencies, damage that propagates through it, and hulls assembled from parts.
milestones.gate: Shoot out a power coupling and watch thrusters on that bus go dead, heat climb, and the affected systems degrade in an order the component graph explains. Repair it and the ship comes back.

milestones.title: Flight model in vacuum and in air
milestones.goal: Flight worth doing. Six-degree thruster allocation solved rather than faked, aerodynamic lift and drag in atmosphere, control surfaces, landing gear, gravity, and the transition between the two regimes.
milestones.gate: Take off from a pad, fly aerodynamically to another continent, exit the atmosphere, manoeuvre in vacuum, re-enter with heating and buffeting, and land on the pad you left. Cockpit view and instruments only.

milestones.title: Seamless travel across a system
milestones.goal: Distance made crossable without a loading screen. Origin rebasing, multi-scale rendering from centimetres to astronomical units, and a high-speed travel mode with a real spool, a real interruption, and a real cost.
milestones.gate: Fly from a planet's surface to a moon of another planet in one continuous shot, with no loading screen, no cut, and no precision artefact anywhere along the path.

milestones.title: Physics at scale and local grids
milestones.goal: The hardest engine problem in the project: walking around inside a ship that is itself moving at speed near a rotating planet. Nested reference frames, which Chaos does not have.
milestones.gate: Walk from the back of a ship to its cockpit while it accelerates, rolls and flies through atmosphere. Set a cup down and it stays on the table. Step out onto a landing pad on a rotating planet and inherit the right frame.

milestones.title: Embodiment and animation
milestones.goal: A body worth being in. Character controller with real momentum, full-body IK, procedural foot and hand placement, first and third person from one skeleton, interaction, seats, ladders, EVA.
milestones.gate: Walk out of a room, climb a ladder, cross a pad in wind, board a ship, take a seat, fly, and get out again — one continuous shot, no cut, no teleport, no animation that slides.

milestones.title: Interiors and modular architecture
milestones.goal: Insides. Ship interiors, station interiors and building interiors built from a modular kit, generated where they should be generated and authored where they should be authored, with no door that is a loading screen.
milestones.gate: Walk from a city street into a building, up through it, out onto a roof pad, into a docked ship and through it to the cockpit, with no load, no fade, and no drop below the frame budget.

milestones.title: Rendering fidelity
milestones.goal: The look. A real PBR material pipeline, lighting that works from a lit cockpit at night to a sunlit dune, volumetrics, decals, wear, post, and the LOD and impostor chain that lets it survive at range.
milestones.gate: Side by side against reference footage at three distances and three lighting conditions, a stranger cannot immediately sort ours from theirs on material and lighting alone.

milestones.title: Asset pipeline and world content
milestones.goal: A way to get content in that is not a person placing things by hand. Import, validation, LOD generation, material assignment, biome and settlement generators, and the tooling to author a system.
milestones.gate: Add a new ship and a new biome end to end through the pipeline, with no manual step outside the tool, and both appear correctly at every LOD.

milestones.title: Performance and optimisation
milestones.goal: Budgets met with everything running at once. Rendering, streaming, physics and memory, at the densities the design actually asks for.
milestones.gate: Sixty frames a second with a full city, a docked ship interior and traffic in view, no frame over 16 ms, and a two-hour session with no memory growth.

milestones.title: Technical vertical slice
milestones.goal: Prove the model. One system, one planet, one moon, one city, one station, three ships — everything above running together and holding up under an hour of unscripted play.
milestones.gate: An hour of free play with no loading screen, no crash, no frame over 16 ms, and nothing that reads as placeholder. This is the milestone the whole technical plan exists to reach.

milestones.title: Simulation core and determinism
milestones.goal: The substrate the living world is written against: event log, reducer contract, snapshots, replay, and a harness that proves reproducibility before there is anything complicated to reproduce.
milestones.gate: Replay a 100,000-tick log twice from one seed and diff the snapshots byte for byte. CI fails on divergence and names the first differing tick.

milestones.title: Agent framework
milestones.goal: The longest simulation milestone, and the one every other system reduces to. Needs, goals, planning, schedules, competence, loyalty — and agents that act on their own beliefs rather than on world state.
milestones.gate: Run 500 agents for 30 simulated days. Any one agent's whole history is explained by its needs and its beliefs, with no appeal to world state it never observed, and two agents holding different beliefs act differently.

milestones.title: Organisation framework
milestones.goal: Membership, roles, holdings, treasury, doctrine and span of control. A player organisation and an NPC organisation are the same type, founded through the same API, subject to the same drift.
milestones.gate: Over-extend an organisation and watch drift appear as subordinates pursuing their own goals — with no code path in the org layer that asks whether the owner is a player.

milestones.title: Economy and logistics
milestones.goal: Goods, markets, production, contracts and convoys. Materials that have to physically arrive, which is what turns a build order into a logistics problem and a convoy into a target.
milestones.gate: A supply shock in one system moves prices three systems away with a lag that matches travel time. Ninety days with no negative inventory and no money created outside a mint event.

milestones.title: Sites, construction and city life
milestones.goal: Claims, construction projects, four utility networks, condition that degrades, maintenance crews that respond, and a first-person tell for every mechanic.
milestones.gate: Build the same habitat archetype on a temperate world and an airless storm moon: different composition and cost from one definition. Cut power to a district and watch life support fail, crews respond, and people put masks on.

milestones.title: Power, threat and coalitions
milestones.goal: The ceiling. Threat models built on belief rather than truth, alarm that rises with believed power and falls with dependency, and coalitions that form because several organisations independently reached one conclusion.
milestones.gate: Grow an organisation until rivals independently cross alarm and form a coalition against it. Feed one member a fabricated belief about another and watch the coalition fracture.

milestones.title: Missions and directives
milestones.goal: Missions generated from tension rather than authored, with stakes that are changes to the world. Directives: standing orders resolved by agents whether or not anyone is watching.
milestones.gate: Every generated mission traces to a named tension between real parties and none has a stake that is only money. A directive left alone for a simulated week resolves through subordinates, correctly or otherwise.

milestones.title: Presence and Command
milestones.goal: The second lens. A map of what your organisation is doing, built from what your people have reported rather than from ground truth, with directives issued from it and your body still standing where you left it.
milestones.gate: Open Command mid-flight: the world does not pause and the ship does not stop. A report three days stale is visibly stale, and a fact nobody has observed does not appear at all.

milestones.title: The living world, integrated
milestones.goal: Everything at once, for a long time, without supervision. This is where the frameworks either compose or they do not.
milestones.gate: Run one simulated year unattended. No runaway monopoly, no dead economy, no organisation with a thousand ships, no agent stuck in a loop, and a dump that still explains itself.

milestones.title: Vertical slice: nothing to coalition
milestones.goal: The game. Arrive with nothing, take work, build a crew, charter an organisation, claim ground, build on it, and grow until the galaxy decides you are the problem.
milestones.gate: A player who has never seen the game goes from nothing to a chartered organisation to a coalition forming against them, in one save, with no tutorial explaining any of the systems.

notes.text: Water rides the terrain quadtree as mesh section 1, inheriting its LOD; quads emitted only where a corner is below sea level
Bug: VertexColor pin 0 is float3 RGB, so masking it for alpha failed to compile. UE logs one line and silently swaps the default material, so every edit to the water shader appeared to do nothing
opaque water, depth-tinted from vertex alpha, Fresnel, SSR-compatible roughness

evidence.caption: Waterline at a shoreline: turquoise shallows, deeper channel, sand — a surface with a horizon
Ocean from orbit with specular sun glint and depth gradient

tasks.title: Wave displacement and shoreline foam
tasks.detail: Crossed Gerstner-style trains, damped in the shallows.
tasks.acceptance: Waves are visible from 200 m and flatten against the shore.

notes.text: Wave phase is Frac(AbsoluteWorldPosition / wavelength), not a plain divide. At a 6371 km radius a world coordinate is ~6.4e8 and float32 has no fractional part left there, so sin() of it returns a staircase. Frac on an absolute world position is the one operation LWC keeps exact. It also rules out the camera-relative position the terrain material uses, which would make the wave field swim with the camera.

First pass keyed foam off a shore band 8 m deep with pow(x,4): a shallow inlet is almost entirely under 8 m, so the whole lagoon went white and read as pack ice. 3 m and pow(x,6) gives a surf line instead. The band doubles as wave damping, so the same number decides where the swell flattens.

tasks.title: Underwater fog and camera transition
tasks.detail: Post-process murk keyed to scene depth, eased on the crossing.
tasks.acceptance: Entering the sea transitions without a pop or a flash.

notes.text: The post-process material failed to compile because SceneTexture outputs float4 and the murk constant is float3 — Lerp between them is not a legal expression. UE answers a failed material with one warning and the default material, and for a post-process blendable that means WorldGridMaterial gets drawn over the entire screen. Second time this failure mode has cost a debugging round; grep the log for 'Failed to compile Material' after every material change.

Murk is applied after tonemapping, so its constant is a final screen value, not a radiance. A physically sensible 0.018 blue rendered as a black screen — there is no exposure left at that point in the pipeline to lift it. 0.05/0.17/0.21 reads as water.

Underwater the sea floor is unlit: the water sheet is section 1 of the same procedural mesh as the terrain, the component casts shadows, and there is no per-section shadow control. Everything below the waterline sits in the water's own shadow. Splitting water into its own component per patch would fix it and also skip collision cooking for water. Blocks anything that wants a visible seabed.

tasks.title: Ocean-floor terrain profile
tasks.detail: Shelf, break, slope, abyssal plain.
tasks.acceptance: A transect from coast to deep ocean shows a shelf break.

notes.text: The seabed was pow(depth, 0.75) — a concave curve, steepest at the shore and flattening outward. That is a bathymetric profile inside out: real ocean floor is a nearly flat shelf, an abrupt break around 140 m, a steep slope to a few kilometres, then an abyssal plain flatter than anything on land. Replaced with those four segments as an explicit piecewise function of the offshore parameter.

The first transect showed no break at all and I nearly retuned the thresholds on the strength of it. The thresholds were fine — the coast search picks its seaward direction by probing six kilometres, which distinguishes water from land and not a basin from a lagoon, so the line ran down the length of an archipelago. Scoring 32 directions on the mean depth of the outer half found open ocean and the break appeared where the profile says it should.

tasks.title: Patch cache keyed by node id
tasks.detail: LRU over released patches, bounded by bytes.
tasks.acceptance: Flying back and forth over a ridge regenerates almost nothing.

notes.text: First version cached at upload time, holding a copy of every patch currently drawn. With ~1000 visible patches at ~700 KB that is most of a gigabyte duplicating what the mesh components already hold, and the budget evicted useful entries to make room for live ones: 4 hits against 4870 generations, 4484 evictions. The cache must hold only what is NOT on screen. Entries are now taken in ReleaseSection and removed again on reuse.

Storing FProcMeshSection rather than the generator's parallel arrays. Taking a copy on release is one memcpy of an interleaved buffer and putting it back is SetProcMeshSection, so nothing is converted in either direction and the arrays the worker produced can still be moved straight into the component.

The first sweep test swept 18 km in 4 seconds — Mach 26. It covered new ground the whole time, generated 13,615 patches and measured streaming throughput, not the cache. A cache can only be tested by a path that repeats: 3 km at 300 m/s gives 86 percent reuse.

tasks.title: Predictive patch prefetch along the velocity vector
tasks.detail: LOD leads the camera. Descent holes fixed; the ascent path regressed and is carried into M01 as the collapse-cascade task.
tasks.acceptance: A 300 m/s descent shows no unfilled patches at any point.

notes.text: Descent holes fixed: 0 holes, starved dropped 107 to 4. Root cause was not prefetch — it was Collapse dropping children before the parent had geometry (the mirror of the split-hold rule), plus a section pool of 2560 against a visible set of 2670. Pool now 3600, jobs in flight 128, and collapse waits for the parent's patch.

NOT DONE: the collapse-hold makes a fast ascent worse — visible nodes 6029, starved 2429, 1444 holes. A rapid climb wants to collapse many levels at once, and each pending node keeps its four children AND requests its own patch, so the visible set inflates exactly when it should be shrinking. Needs collapse to run bottom-up in one step per frame, or a pending-collapse budget. Re-home this in the reworked roadmap.
Ascent-path regression, see notes. Carrying into the reworked roadmap.

tasks.title: Fix the collapse cascade the prefetch work exposed
tasks.detail: A fast ascent wants to collapse many levels at once. Each pending node keeps its four children and also requests its own patch, so the visible set inflates exactly when it should shrink: 6,029 nodes, 2,429 starved, 1,444 holes. Collapse has to resolve bottom-up within a frame budget.
tasks.acceptance: A full-thrust climb from ground to orbit reports zero holes and a visible set that falls monotonically.

notes.text: Two causes, neither of them the prefetch. Collapse dropped children before the parent had geometry (the mirror of the split-hold rule), and the section pool was 2560 against a visible set of 2670. Pool now 3600, jobs in flight 128, and collapse resolves bottom-up: the intent is pushed down the subtree and only the level whose children are leaves requests geometry.

Holding children while waiting for the parent's patch is a deadlock, not a delay: the four children hold sections from the same pool the parent needs one from. It surfaced as 1,500 patches of unfillable demand growing for as long as the climb lasted. The wait is now bounded at 90 frames, after which the node collapses anyway and accepts a transient hole. A hole for a few frames beats a tree that never shrinks.
The prefetch lead was clamped against altitude alone, so at 300 km up three seconds of climb led 150 km sideways and subdivided a region nobody was flying to. Now clamped to 5 km absolute as well.

Residual: 8 holes worst during the climb, against a visible set of 2,800 falling to 405. Not literally zero, and the acceptance line says zero — the remainder is one or two frames at the moment the attitude change starts. Recording it rather than rounding it.

tasks.title: Frame-time recording in the scripted flight
tasks.detail: Every run writes out/performance.txt: per-phase mean, median, p95, p99 and max, with game, render and GPU thread time beside them, and a verdict against the budget. A screenshot has no frame time in it, which is how a run at nineteen frames a second passed twenty-six task reviews.
tasks.acceptance: Every scripted run produces a report with a PASS or FAIL verdict, and a stall over 33 ms is logged with its timestamp and phase.

notes.text: Built because the user noticed the landing lagged and the captures had shown nothing wrong for twenty-six tasks. The first report: 19 fps mean, 5-7 fps at the surface, 99.6 percent of frames over budget. Screenshots do not have a frame time in them.

tasks.title: Cut the volumetric cloud cost
tasks.detail: ProfileGPU at the worst point put VolumetricCloud at 90 ms of a 130 ms frame — 68 percent — from a sample scale of 2.0 against a 400 km tracing distance. Twice the engine's samples over eight times its distance.
tasks.acceptance: Cloud cost falls below 15 ms at ground level with no visible change in the deck from a kilometre up.

notes.text: ProfileGPU at the surface: VolumetricCloud CloudView 90.2 ms of a 130 ms frame, 68 percent, on a 334x188 buffer. ViewSampleCountScale was 2.0 against TracingMaxDistance 400 km — twice the engine's samples over eight times its distance, and the cost is the product.

0.35 samples over 55 km. Surface frame 137 to 53 ms, overall mean 53 to 41 ms. Clouds are now roughly 12 ms; the remaining GPU cost is TSR at Epic quality (11 ms), GBufferClear (9 ms) and deferred lighting (6 ms). Still 25 fps against a 60 fps budget — this bought a factor of 2.6, not the answer.

tasks.acceptance: A 60-degree face reads as rock with bedding, and there is debris at its foot that was not placed by hand.

tasks.acceptance: Ten thousand visible instances at 60 fps, identical placement across runs, and nothing floating or half-buried.

tasks.title: Vegetation with wind response
tasks.detail: Trees and grass that move with the wind field M04 will provide, and stop moving when it stops.
tasks.acceptance: Wind speed changes and vegetation responds within a second, at every LOD including the impostor.

tasks.title: Far-field impostors and horizon detail
tasks.detail: Beyond the last real LOD, the planet needs to keep its silhouette. Impostors for scatter, and a horizon that does not go smooth.
tasks.acceptance: A mountain range 80 km away has a silhouette and reads as terrain rather than as a gradient.

tasks.title: Snow, ice and seasonal cover
tasks.detail: Cover driven by the climate field and the season, accumulating by altitude and latitude, affecting material and scatter.
tasks.acceptance: The same location has snow in winter and not in summer, and the snow line moves with altitude.

tasks.title: Terrain sampling API with a stable contract
tasks.detail: One place gameplay asks for height, normal, biome, slope and material at a point, agreeing exactly with what is rendered. Everything built after this depends on it.
tasks.acceptance: A thousand random queries agree with a physics trace to the millimetre.

tasks.title: Terrain modification API
tasks.detail: Levelling, excavation and fill, persisted as a sparse delta over the generated field. Construction in M19 needs ground it can flatten.
tasks.acceptance: Flatten a pad, reload, and it is still flat; the delta costs nothing where nothing was modified.

tasks.title: Streaming budget manager
tasks.detail: One authority deciding how much generation, cooking and upload happens per frame, with the budget split by priority rather than first come first served.
tasks.acceptance: Under deliberate overload, the frame budget holds and the degradation is in detail rather than in holes.

tasks.title: Shadow-specific terrain LOD
tasks.detail: Shadow casters do not need the LOD the camera needs, and paying full resolution into a shadow map is most of a cascade wasted.
tasks.acceptance: Shadow cost drops measurably with no visible change in shadow quality.

tasks.title: Disk cache for generated patches
tasks.detail: Generation is deterministic, so it need only happen once per machine. A content-addressed on-disk cache under the terrain cache.
tasks.acceptance: A second visit to the same ground generates nothing and is bit-identical.

tasks.title: Terrain debug visualisers
tasks.detail: LOD level, patch boundaries, collision presence, biome, climate fields, cache state, streaming queue — all toggleable in-game.
tasks.acceptance: Every terrain bug class in M00's history is diagnosable from the visualisers without adding code.

tasks.title: Terrain regression suite
tasks.detail: Automated flights over fixed seeds producing captures and metrics, compared against references. Holes, cracks, popping and budget overruns all become build failures.
tasks.acceptance: Each of those four failure modes, introduced deliberately, is caught by CI.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the 200 km transect
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The milestone gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: 200 km at 300 m and 900 m/s: no holes, no seams, no frame over 16 ms, collision present throughout.

tasks.title: Body definition: mass, radius, rotation, tilt, orbit
tasks.detail: One description a planet, moon, station or asteroid is built from, in double precision, deterministic from seed.
tasks.acceptance: A system description round-trips through serialisation and rebuilds identically.

tasks.title: Keplerian ephemeris
tasks.detail: Position and velocity of every body at any time, from orbital elements. Analytic rather than integrated, so there is no drift and no need to simulate the solar system to know where a moon was last Tuesday.
tasks.acceptance: Positions at t agree whether computed forward from zero or directly, to sub-metre over a simulated century.

tasks.title: Reference frame hierarchy
tasks.detail: System, body, surface and vehicle frames with transforms between them. Everything positional in the project ends up expressed in one of these, and getting it wrong later is unaffordable.
tasks.acceptance: A point on a rotating planet's surface transformed to system frame and back is unchanged to the millimetre.

tasks.title: Rotation, day and night from the real rotation rate
tasks.detail: Sun position derived from the body's rotation and orbit, not from a time-of-day slider.
tasks.acceptance: Local noon happens when the ephemeris says the sun is at its highest, at any latitude and any date.

tasks.title: Axial tilt and seasons
tasks.detail: Tilt drives insolation, which drives the climate field from M02 and the snow line with it.
tasks.acceptance: A high-latitude site has a measurably shorter day in winter and its snow line moves across a simulated year.

tasks.title: Multi-body rendering with correct illumination
tasks.detail: Other planets and moons visible in the sky, at the right place, with the right phase and the right apparent size.
tasks.acceptance: A moon's phase matches the sun-moon-observer geometry at any time and from any body in the system.

tasks.title: Eclipses and body shadows
tasks.detail: A moon casting a shadow on a planet, a planet eclipsing its moon, and the lighting change on the ground when it happens.
tasks.acceptance: An eclipse predicted by the ephemeris is observable from the surface at the predicted time, and the ground goes dark.

tasks.title: The star as a physical light
tasks.detail: Intensity, colour temperature and angular size from the star's class and the observer's distance — so an inner planet is genuinely brighter and an outer one genuinely dimmer.
tasks.acceptance: Illuminance at each planet matches the inverse-square prediction, and auto-exposure handles the range without clipping.

tasks.title: Star field from a generated catalogue
tasks.detail: Stars with position, magnitude and colour, correct for the observer's location in the galaxy, and parallax between systems.
tasks.acceptance: The same constellations appear from two planets in one system, and measurably differ between systems.

tasks.title: Moons on the shared terrain framework
tasks.detail: A moon is a body with a different radius, no atmosphere and different climate inputs. If it needs its own renderer, the framework is wrong.
tasks.acceptance: Land on a moon using the same terrain code path, with correct low gravity and no atmosphere.

tasks.title: Gas giants
tasks.detail: Volumetric banding, storms, and a surface you can descend into until pressure ends the attempt.
tasks.acceptance: Descend into a gas giant: bands resolve, pressure rises, and the ship is destroyed at the depth the atmosphere model predicts.

tasks.title: Ring systems
tasks.detail: Particle rings with self-shadowing and a shadow cast on the planet, flyable through rather than a texture on a disc.
tasks.acceptance: Fly through a ring plane: density resolves into particles and the ring's shadow moves across the planet correctly.

tasks.title: Asteroid fields and small irregular bodies
tasks.detail: Non-spherical bodies need a different mesh path from the cube-sphere, and orbits that are individually tracked rather than instanced.
tasks.acceptance: Land on an irregular asteroid with correct local gravity direction at every point on its surface.

tasks.title: Orbital stations and platforms
tasks.detail: Structures on rails around a body, with their own local frame that things can dock to and stand in.
tasks.acceptance: A station's position matches its orbit over a simulated month, and a docked ship stays docked.

tasks.title: Gravity field from real masses
tasks.detail: Inverse-square from every significant body rather than one hardcoded constant, including the transition between spheres of influence.
tasks.acceptance: A ship coasting between two bodies follows the trajectory the two-body model predicts, and the dominant body switches cleanly.

tasks.title: System generation from seed
tasks.detail: Star class, planet count, orbits, compositions and moons, generated to be plausible rather than uniform — hot rocks close in, gas giants further out, habitable zones where the star puts them.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty generated systems are all physically plausible and none is a rearrangement of another.

tasks.title: Time acceleration for testing
tasks.detail: Run the ephemeris and climate at a thousand times normal so a year can be inspected in minutes, without the renderer trying to keep up.
tasks.acceptance: A simulated year runs in under a minute and ends in the state the analytic model predicts.

tasks.title: Ephemeris determinism and agreement tests
tasks.detail: Two processes, one seed, identical positions; and the sky agrees with the ephemeris at a hundred random times and places.
tasks.acceptance: Sky and ephemeris agree to the arcminute in every sample.

tasks.title: System map and query API
tasks.detail: What is where, how far, how long to get there. The Command lens in M22 is a view over this and so is every travel decision before it.
tasks.acceptance: Travel time between any two sites is queryable and matches what actually flying it takes.

tasks.title: Playable proof: watch a moon transit and then fly to it
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: A moon rises, transits and sets on schedule; then it is flown to and landed on, in one session.

tasks.title: Atmosphere profile per body
tasks.detail: Composition, surface pressure, scale height and lapse rate as data. Earth's numbers become one row rather than the only row.
tasks.acceptance: Three bodies with different atmospheres render correctly from ground and orbit from data alone.

tasks.title: Scattering for non-Earth compositions
tasks.detail: Rayleigh and Mie coefficients derived from composition, so a CO2 sky is the colour physics says and not the colour someone liked.
tasks.acceptance: A thin CO2 atmosphere produces a butterscotch sky and a blue sunset, from composition alone.

tasks.title: Volumetric fog that is not planar
tasks.detail: Exponential height fog fills space from orbit because it has no notion of a sphere. Ground fog, valley inversion and haze need a volumetric layer bound to the body.
tasks.acceptance: Fog fills a valley at dawn, is absent on the ridge above it, and is invisible from orbit.

tasks.title: Pressure-cell weather model
tasks.detail: A coarse global field of pressure cells advected by rotation, producing wind, fronts and storm systems that move and evolve. Deterministic from seed and time.
tasks.acceptance: A storm system tracked over a simulated week follows a coherent path, and the same seed reproduces it exactly.

tasks.title: Wind field queryable by everything
tasks.detail: Speed and direction at any point and altitude, read by flight, vegetation, particles, audio and the settlement layer.
tasks.acceptance: All five consumers respond to the same wind change within a second.

tasks.title: Cloud layers at real altitudes
tasks.detail: Multiple volumetric decks — low cumulus, mid, high cirrus — at altitudes the atmosphere profile determines, advected by the wind field.
tasks.acceptance: Climb through three distinct cloud decks at the altitudes the profile predicts, and see them layered correctly from orbit.

tasks.title: Precipitation: rain, snow and dust
tasks.detail: Driven by the weather model, rendered volumetrically and as surface effects, with the type decided by temperature and composition.
tasks.acceptance: A front crosses a site: rain at low altitude, snow above the freezing level, and the boundary sits where the lapse rate puts it.

tasks.title: Surface wetness, puddles and drying
tasks.detail: Rain changes roughness and colour, water collects where the terrain says it should, and it dries at a rate the temperature decides.
tasks.acceptance: After rain the ground is visibly wet, puddles sit in hollows, and both resolve over an hour of game time.

tasks.title: Storms: lightning, dust and severe weather
tasks.detail: The extreme tail of the weather model, with the visual and audio signature to match, and enough force to matter to a ship.
tasks.acceptance: A severe storm is dangerous to fly through and visible as a storm from orbit in the same place.

tasks.title: Turbulence and wind loading on vehicles
tasks.detail: Wind shear, gusts and thermals as forces on the flight model, not as camera shake.
tasks.acceptance: Crossing a mountain range in high wind requires control input, and the forces come from the wind field rather than from a random number.

tasks.title: Temperature and pressure as physical fields
tasks.detail: Queryable at any point, driven by latitude, altitude, season and weather. Life support, materials, habitability and building composition all read from this one source.
tasks.acceptance: Temperature at a point matches the lapse-rate prediction, and the settlement layer reads the same number the renderer does.

tasks.title: Re-entry heating from atmospheric density
tasks.detail: Heating as a function of density and velocity, with the visual effect and the ship damage both derived from it rather than triggered by altitude.
tasks.acceptance: A steep re-entry burns and a shallow one does not, and the difference is the density-velocity integral.

tasks.title: Cockpit and visor effects
tasks.detail: Rain streaks that respond to airspeed, dust accumulation, icing, fogging, and the wipers or heaters that clear them.
tasks.acceptance: Fly through rain and the canopy streaks; accelerate and the streaks run backward; turn on the heater and fogging clears.

tasks.title: Environmental audio
tasks.detail: Wind by speed and air density, precipitation on surfaces, thunder delayed by distance, and silence in vacuum.
tasks.acceptance: Wind noise scales with dynamic pressure and stops entirely above the atmosphere.

tasks.title: Aurora at magnetic poles
tasks.detail: Driven by the body's magnetic field and stellar activity, visible from the ground and from orbit.
tasks.acceptance: Aurora appears at high latitude during a modelled solar event and not otherwise.

tasks.title: Weather forecast API
tasks.detail: What the weather will be at a place and time. Flight planning, settlement shutters and mission generation all need to anticipate rather than react.
tasks.acceptance: A forecast issued six hours ahead matches what happens, within the model's stated confidence.

tasks.title: Volumetric performance budget
tasks.detail: Clouds, fog and precipitation are the easiest way to lose the frame. Resolution, temporal reprojection and distance-based quality, under one budget.
tasks.acceptance: Worst-case weather costs no more than 4 ms and degrades in detail rather than in frame rate.

tasks.title: Weather determinism and orbit-to-ground agreement
tasks.detail: Same seed and time gives the same weather, and the storm seen from orbit is the storm flown into.
tasks.acceptance: Both properties hold across a hundred sampled times and places.

tasks.title: Playable proof: fly into a storm front
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Visibility, wind loading and audio change together on entry, and the same storm is in the same place from orbit.

tasks.title: Ship definition format
tasks.detail: A ship is data: hull geometry, hardpoints, component slots, mass distribution, and the topology that connects them. Adding a ship must never require a compiler.
tasks.acceptance: A new ship is one data file plus art, and it flies.

tasks.title: Component graph with typed ports
tasks.detail: Components connect through typed ports — power, coolant, fuel, data — and the graph is what damage, heat and failure propagate through. This is the spine of the whole milestone.
tasks.acceptance: A component's inputs and outputs are discoverable at runtime and an unsatisfiable connection is a load error, not a crash.

tasks.title: Power generation and distribution
tasks.detail: Plants, buses, priorities and brownouts. Demand exceeding supply sheds load in priority order rather than stopping the ship.
tasks.acceptance: Overload a bus and the lowest-priority consumers drop first, in the order the configuration states.

tasks.title: Thermal model
tasks.detail: Components generate heat, coolant loops move it, radiators reject it, and an overheated component throttles or fails. Heat is also a signature.
tasks.acceptance: Run at full power with radiators retracted and the ship overheats on the schedule the thermal model predicts.

tasks.title: Fuel: types, tanks, transfer, consumption
tasks.detail: Propellant and reactor fuel as separate resources, consumed at rates the flight model produces rather than at a rate someone picked.
tasks.acceptance: Fuel burn integrated over a flight matches thrust integrated over the same flight, and running dry stops the engines.

tasks.title: Mass, centre of mass and inertia from contents
tasks.detail: Computed from hull, components, fuel and cargo, updating as fuel burns and cargo moves. An unevenly loaded ship handles unevenly.
tasks.acceptance: Load cargo on one side and the ship's handling changes measurably in the direction predicted.

tasks.title: Damage model over the component graph
tasks.detail: Hits damage components, damage propagates along ports, and the failure order is explained by the topology rather than by a table.
tasks.acceptance: Destroying a power coupling kills exactly the components downstream of it and nothing else.

tasks.title: Hull damage: penetration, deformation, breach
tasks.detail: Localised hull state, with pressure loss where the hull is breached and structural failure where enough of it is gone.
tasks.acceptance: A breach vents the compartment behind it and not the rest of the ship.

tasks.title: Component wear and condition
tasks.detail: Components degrade with use and with abuse, changing performance before they fail. The maintenance loop in M19 reads from this.
tasks.acceptance: A neglected thruster loses measurable output over a hundred hours of operation and warns before it fails.

tasks.title: Repair and component replacement
tasks.detail: Field repair with limited effect, workshop repair with full effect, and component swapping with the parts economy in mind.
tasks.acceptance: A damaged ship is repaired to a stated condition and the parts are consumed from somewhere.

tasks.title: Life support as a component
tasks.detail: Atmosphere, pressure and temperature inside the hull, with consumption, reserves and failure. On a breathable world it is a convenience; elsewhere it is the thing keeping you alive.
tasks.acceptance: Cut life support in vacuum and the internal atmosphere depletes on the modelled schedule, with warnings.

tasks.title: Shields
tasks.detail: Directional shields with capacity, recharge, and a power draw that competes with everything else on the bus.
tasks.acceptance: Raising shields measurably reduces power available to thrust, and the trade-off is visible on the instruments.

tasks.title: Signature model: thermal, electromagnetic, cross-section
tasks.detail: What a ship looks like to a sensor, derived from what it is doing. Running cold and quiet must be a real option, because information is the design's scarce commodity.
tasks.acceptance: Shutting down non-essential systems measurably reduces detection range, and the numbers come from the thermal and power models.

tasks.title: Hardpoints and mount framework
tasks.detail: The general mechanism for attaching things to a hull — weapons, mining gear, sensors, cargo pods — with size classes and power and cooling draw. Not the weapons themselves.
tasks.acceptance: A mount accepts any component of its class, refuses others, and its power and heat appear in the ship's totals.

tasks.title: Cargo hold and volumetric stowage
tasks.detail: Cargo occupies space and has mass and a position. A full hold is visibly full and an unbalanced one is felt.
tasks.acceptance: Loading to capacity is limited by volume or mass, whichever binds first, and the contents are visible in the hold.

tasks.title: Animated ship parts as components
tasks.detail: Gear, ramps, doors, radiators and canopies are components with state, power draw and failure modes, not animations.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting power mid-cycle leaves the gear half-deployed and it stays there until power returns.

tasks.title: Power-on and shutdown sequence
tasks.detail: A ship starts cold and comes up in an order the component graph implies. This is where a ship stops being a vehicle and becomes a machine.
tasks.acceptance: Cold start brings systems up in dependency order, and skipping a step prevents the next one.

tasks.title: Instrumentation framework
tasks.detail: Multi-function displays driven by real component state through one data path. An instrument that lies is a bug in the instrument, not in the display.
tasks.acceptance: Every gauge traces to a component reading, and a failed sensor makes its gauge unavailable rather than wrong.

tasks.title: Ship audio from component state
tasks.detail: Engine note from throttle and load, coolant pumps under thermal stress, alarms from the systems that raised them.
tasks.acceptance: A listener can identify which subsystem is in trouble from audio alone.

tasks.title: Damage visuals
tasks.detail: Scorching, deformation, venting, sparks and debris tied to the damage state rather than played as effects.
tasks.acceptance: A ship's exterior condition is readable at a glance and matches its component state.

tasks.title: Ship configuration and outfitting
tasks.detail: Swap components within slot and power constraints, with the consequences computed rather than listed.
tasks.acceptance: Fitting an oversized power plant changes mass, heat and handling, and the configuration screen shows all three before it is fitted.

tasks.title: Ship state persistence
tasks.detail: Condition, fuel, cargo, damage and configuration survive a save, a reload and eventually a handover to the simulation.
tasks.acceptance: A damaged, half-fuelled, oddly configured ship reloads exactly as it was.

tasks.title: Ship diagnostics and test harness
tasks.detail: A headless rig that builds a ship, applies loads and damage, and asserts the component graph behaves. Ship bugs are systemic and need systemic tests.
tasks.acceptance: Every failure mode in this milestone has a test that reproduces it without flying anything.

tasks.title: Playable proof: shoot out a power coupling
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Thrusters on that bus go dead, heat climbs, systems degrade in graph order, and repair brings the ship back.

tasks.title: Rigid-body integration with a real inertia tensor
tasks.detail: Replace the prototype's hand-integrated point mass with a proper rigid body using the mass distribution M05 computes. Still hand-integrated rather than handed to Chaos, for the reasons in SS6.9.
tasks.acceptance: Angular response matches the inertia tensor, and an off-axis thrust produces the torque the geometry predicts.

tasks.title: Thruster allocation solver
tasks.detail: Given thruster positions, orientations and limits, solve for the combination producing the commanded force and torque. This is what makes a ship's handling a consequence of its thruster layout rather than of a handling number.
tasks.acceptance: Disable a thruster and the solver compensates, with the loss of authority in the axis the geometry predicts.

tasks.title: Flight assist and control modes
tasks.detail: Assist on, assist off, coupled and decoupled, each a different controller over the same allocator rather than a different flight model.
tasks.acceptance: Switching modes changes only the controller; the physics underneath is identical and provably so.

tasks.title: Aerodynamics: lift, drag and control surfaces
tasks.detail: Real aerodynamic forces from angle of attack, airspeed and the atmospheric density M04 provides, with control surfaces that only work in air.
tasks.acceptance: A winged ship glides unpowered in atmosphere and does not in vacuum.

tasks.title: Stall, spin and recovery
tasks.detail: An aerodynamic envelope with edges. Exceeding them has consequences that can be recovered from if the pilot knows how.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberate stall departs controlled flight and standard recovery inputs recover it.

tasks.title: Vacuum-to-atmosphere transition
tasks.detail: Aerodynamic authority fades in as density rises and thruster authority does not, so the handover is continuous rather than a mode change.
tasks.acceptance: A re-entry from vacuum to sea level shows no discontinuity in forces at any altitude.

tasks.title: VTOL and hover
tasks.detail: Vertical thrust with ground effect, and the fuel cost that makes hovering a decision rather than a default.
tasks.acceptance: Hovering consumes fuel at the rate thrust-to-weight implies, and ground effect is measurable near the surface.

tasks.title: Landing gear and ground handling
tasks.detail: Suspension, contact, friction, braking and steering on the ground. Landing is a physical event, not a state change.
tasks.acceptance: A hard landing compresses the gear and can damage it; a shallow one does not; the ship stays put on a slope up to the friction limit.

tasks.title: G-force model and pilot effects
tasks.detail: Sustained and transient acceleration on the pilot, with the visual and physiological limits that make manoeuvres have a cost.
tasks.acceptance: A sustained high-g turn greys the view on the modelled schedule and recovery follows the same model.

tasks.title: Flight computer limits and envelope protection
tasks.detail: Configurable limits on the allocator — g, angular rate, thermal — that a pilot can relax at their own risk.
tasks.acceptance: Limits are enforced by the controller, and disabling them lets the airframe be damaged.

tasks.title: Autopilot framework
tasks.detail: Hold attitude, hold altitude, hold station, approach and auto-land, as controllers over the same allocator. Directives in M21 will drive ships through this.
tasks.acceptance: Auto-land puts a ship on a pad in wind, repeatably, from any approach.

tasks.title: Docking
tasks.detail: Approach corridors, alignment, capture and release against a station or another ship, with the moving-frame handover M08 will formalise.
tasks.acceptance: Dock with a station in orbit and the ship's frame becomes the station's with no jolt.

tasks.title: Ground vehicle framework
tasks.detail: Wheeled and tracked vehicles over the same rigid body and the same terrain collision, because a settlement needs things that are not ships.
tasks.acceptance: A ground vehicle drives across terrain with suspension responding to the surface the renderer draws.

tasks.title: Input framework: HOTAS, gamepad, mouse and keyboard
tasks.detail: One binding layer over one command set, with curves, deadzones and per-device profiles. Not three control schemes.
tasks.acceptance: All three devices produce identical commanded forces for equivalent input, and rebinding requires no code.

tasks.title: HUD and flight instruments
tasks.detail: Velocity vector, attitude, target reticle, energy, and the instruments a pilot actually flies on — driven through M05's instrumentation path.
tasks.acceptance: A full flight is completable on instruments alone with the external view disabled.

tasks.title: Collision response for vehicles
tasks.detail: Impacts transfer momentum and damage components through M05's graph, rather than triggering a generic effect.
tasks.acceptance: A glancing impact damages the components at the point of contact and imparts the momentum the collision implies.

tasks.title: Ship-to-ship physical interaction
tasks.detail: Ships push each other, land on each other, and carry each other. The prerequisite for M08's nested frames.
tasks.acceptance: A small ship lands on a large one and is carried with it.

tasks.title: Flight recorder
tasks.detail: Record every input, force and state to a file that can be replayed exactly. Flight bugs are transient and unreproducible without this.
tasks.acceptance: A recorded flight replays to an identical trajectory.

tasks.title: Flight model tuning tools
tasks.detail: In-editor visualisation of thruster authority, aerodynamic forces, envelope and control response, so tuning is measured rather than felt.
tasks.acceptance: A ship's envelope can be read off a chart the tool generates.

tasks.title: Flight regression suite
tasks.detail: Recorded flights replayed in CI with trajectory tolerances, so a physics change that alters handling is caught immediately.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberate one-percent thrust change fails the suite.

tasks.title: Playable proof: continent, orbit, pad
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Pad to another continent aerodynamically, out to vacuum, manoeuvre, re-enter with heating, land on the pad you left — cockpit only.

tasks.title: Origin rebasing
tasks.detail: Move the world under the camera so float precision never has to express an astronomical unit. The prototype avoids this by keeping vertices patch-relative; everything else in the game will not have that luxury.
tasks.acceptance: At one AU from origin, a one-millimetre movement is still one millimetre, for every actor and every particle system.

tasks.title: Depth precision across twelve orders of magnitude
tasks.detail: A cockpit instrument at 40 cm and a planet at 400,000 km in one frame. Reversed-Z with cascaded depth ranges, or a logarithmic buffer, chosen by measurement rather than by preference.
tasks.acceptance: No z-fighting anywhere from a hand-held object to a planet on the same screen.

tasks.title: Scale-aware camera and rendering
tasks.detail: Near and far rendering passes composited, so distant bodies are drawn at a scale the depth buffer can hold.
tasks.acceptance: A planet, its moon and a ship's own hull are all correctly occluded against each other.

tasks.title: Entity relevance and streaming by distance
tasks.detail: What exists, what is simulated, what is rendered, and what is a dot — with explicit bands and explicit transitions between them.
tasks.acceptance: A ship a thousand kilometres away is a dot; approach it and it becomes a ship with no pop and no state loss.

tasks.title: High-speed travel mode
tasks.detail: The thing that makes a system crossable in minutes rather than weeks: spool time, alignment, a speed that scales with distance, and a real cost.
tasks.acceptance: Cross the system in a few minutes, with every phase interruptible and the ship in a legal physical state at every instant.

tasks.title: Interdiction and interruption
tasks.detail: High-speed travel can be pulled out of, by mass, by another ship, or by failure — otherwise the entire strategic layer has no chokepoints.
tasks.acceptance: A ship in transit is pulled out at the position and velocity the model predicts, and the pursuer arrives with it.

tasks.title: Route planning and navigation
tasks.detail: Plot a route between any two sites, with time, fuel and hazard estimates that match what flying it actually costs.
tasks.acceptance: Estimated and actual travel time agree within five percent over twenty sampled routes.

tasks.title: Interstellar travel
tasks.detail: Between systems: whatever mechanism the fiction settles on, with a duration that keeps information genuinely slow. Design SS8: instant travel means instant information and there is no game left.
tasks.acceptance: An interstellar transit takes a stated time, is interruptible, and leaves the destination system correctly streamed on arrival.

tasks.title: Arrival and approach handling
tasks.detail: Deceleration, traffic separation, approach clearance and the transition into a body's frame — the part where seamlessness usually breaks.
tasks.acceptance: Arrive at a planet from high speed and descend to a pad without a single frame over budget.

tasks.title: Cross-scale physics stability
tasks.detail: Physics at 200 m/s near a rotating planet and at high speed between them, without tunnelling, jitter or integration blow-up.
tasks.acceptance: A twenty-minute transit ends with position error inside tolerance and no jitter at any point.

tasks.title: Bookmarks, waypoints and the navigation UI
tasks.detail: Somewhere to point the ship at, including places the player named and places they were told about.
tasks.acceptance: A waypoint set from the map is flyable to and arrives where it said.

tasks.title: Traffic: other ships going about their business
tasks.detail: Ships on routes, arriving and departing, at a density the streaming budget supports. Placeholder behaviour now; the simulation drives it from M16.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty ships operate in one system without a frame cost that reads on a graph.

tasks.title: Precision and seam regression suite
tasks.detail: Automated traversals at many scales asserting no precision artefact, no hitch over a threshold, and no discontinuity in position or velocity.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberately reintroduced precision bug is caught by CI.

tasks.title: Hitch elimination pass
tasks.detail: Every remaining stall over 4 ms during traversal, found and removed. Seamless is a property that is destroyed by one hitch.
tasks.acceptance: A full system traversal shows no frame over 16 ms and no allocation spike over the budget.

tasks.title: Playable proof: surface to a moon of another planet
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded in one continuous shot.
tasks.acceptance: No loading screen, no cut, no precision artefact anywhere on the path.

tasks.title: Spike: three approaches to nested reference frames
tasks.detail: Chaos with a moving kinematic parent, a second physics scene per grid with transform bridging, or a custom solver for grid-local bodies. Build enough of each to measure, then decide in an ADR. Choosing wrong here is a year.
tasks.acceptance: Three prototypes, measured on stability, cost and integration risk, and an ADR that picks one and says why.

tasks.title: Local physics grid framework
tasks.detail: A grid is a moving frame with its own physics content. Bodies inside it are simulated in grid-local coordinates, so a ship at 3,000 m/s is a room at rest.
tasks.acceptance: An object at rest inside a manoeuvring ship stays at rest relative to the ship, at any speed the ship can reach.

tasks.title: Frame entry and exit
tasks.detail: Walking onto a ship, stepping off onto a pad, a ship entering another ship's hold — velocity and angular velocity transferred correctly at every boundary.
tasks.acceptance: Step from a landing pad onto a hovering ship and back with no jolt, no launch, and no lost velocity.

tasks.title: Character controller inside a moving frame
tasks.detail: Walking, standing and falling relative to a frame that is itself accelerating and rotating, with the apparent forces that implies.
tasks.acceptance: Walk the length of a ship while it accelerates and rolls, without sliding and without the controller fighting the frame.

tasks.title: Apparent forces: acceleration, rotation, Coriolis
tasks.detail: Inertia felt inside an accelerating ship, and centrifugal gravity inside a rotating station with the Coriolis effect that comes with it.
tasks.acceptance: A dropped object inside a spinning station lands where the rotating frame predicts, not directly below.

tasks.title: Nested grids
tasks.detail: A vehicle inside a ship inside a station. Depth-limited, but the limit must be a decision rather than an accident.
tasks.acceptance: Two levels of nesting are stable and the limit is enforced with a clear error rather than a failure.

tasks.title: Gravity generation inside grids
tasks.detail: Artificial gravity as a per-grid field with orientation, plus what happens when it fails and everything inside becomes free-floating.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting grid gravity leaves loose objects and characters floating with the velocity they had.

tasks.title: Continuous collision detection at high speed
tasks.detail: Nothing may pass through a hull because it moved far in one step. Sweeps for fast bodies, with a budget.
tasks.acceptance: A projectile at any modelled speed always hits the surface it should, over ten thousand trials.

tasks.title: Collision geometry for large structures
tasks.detail: Ships and stations need collision at a fidelity that supports walking inside them, streamed, without cooking a battleship every time one appears.
tasks.acceptance: A large ship's interior collision streams in ahead of the character and never blocks a frame.

tasks.title: Constraint and joint framework
tasks.detail: Doors, ramps, turrets, elevators, landing gear and cargo clamps as constraints driven by M05's components rather than as animations.
tasks.acceptance: A ramp lowered under load moves at the rate the actuator provides and stops when the power does.

tasks.title: Object handling: pick up, carry, place, throw
tasks.detail: Loose objects with mass that behave inside moving frames, because a cup on a table in a manoeuvring ship is the whole promise of this milestone.
tasks.acceptance: Set a cup on a table, fly a barrel roll, and the cup behaves the way the frame and the friction say it should.

tasks.title: Ragdoll and character physics
tasks.detail: Bodies that fall, are thrown and collide, correctly inside a moving frame.
tasks.acceptance: A ragdoll inside an accelerating ship slides toward the stern at the rate the acceleration implies.

tasks.title: Destruction framework
tasks.detail: Structural damage to ships, buildings and terrain features, with debris that is physical and then is not, on a budget.
tasks.acceptance: A destroyed structure produces debris that settles and is cleaned up without a frame cost that reads on a graph.

tasks.title: Physics determinism and stability harness
tasks.detail: Fixed-step physics with recorded scenarios replayed in CI. Frame-rate dependent physics is a bug that only shows on someone else's machine.
tasks.acceptance: A recorded scenario replays identically at 30, 60 and 144 fps.

tasks.title: Physics performance budget
tasks.detail: Grid count, body count and substep cost under one budget, with degradation that is a decision rather than a stutter.
tasks.acceptance: Ten active grids with two hundred bodies each stays inside the physics budget.

tasks.title: Playable proof: walk to the cockpit at speed
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Walk from the stern to the cockpit while the ship accelerates, rolls and flies through atmosphere; a cup set down stays on the table; step out onto a pad on a rotating planet and inherit the right frame.

tasks.title: Character controller with momentum
tasks.detail: Acceleration, deceleration, turning radius and footing rather than a capsule that changes velocity instantly. A body has mass and the controller has to admit it.
tasks.acceptance: Stopping from a run takes distance, turning at speed carries momentum, and neither is a curve someone drew.

tasks.title: One skeleton for first and third person
tasks.detail: Two skeletons is two sets of bugs and a first person view whose body is a lie. One rig, camera attached to the head, IK correcting what the camera can see.
tasks.acceptance: Look down in first person and see the same body a third-person camera sees, doing the same thing.

tasks.title: Full-body IK and foot placement
tasks.detail: Feet land on the ground that is actually there, at the angle it is at, on stairs, slopes and debris.
tasks.acceptance: Walk across broken terrain and a stairway with no foot sliding and no foot intersecting geometry.

tasks.title: Locomotion state machine and blend framework
tasks.detail: Idle, walk, run, sprint, crouch, prone, strafe, turn-in-place, with distance-matched transitions rather than fixed blends.
tasks.acceptance: No locomotion transition slides the feet, at any speed or direction change.

tasks.title: Locomotion in variable gravity
tasks.detail: Walking on a moon, in a station's spin gravity, and in a ship under thrust — stride, jump arc and fall speed all derived from local gravity.
tasks.acceptance: The same controller produces correct movement at 0.16 g, 1 g and 1.5 g with no special-cased animation.

tasks.title: Zero-gravity movement and EVA
tasks.detail: Push off, drift, arrest with a thruster pack, grab handholds. A different control problem, not a different character.
tasks.acceptance: Cross a compartment in zero gravity by pushing off and catching a handhold, with momentum conserved throughout.

tasks.title: Interaction framework
tasks.detail: One mechanism for everything a person can touch: buttons, levers, doors, seats, terminals, containers. Highlighting, reach, occlusion and the animation that sells it.
tasks.acceptance: A new interactable is one data declaration and inherits highlighting, reach and animation with no bespoke code.

tasks.title: Seats, harnesses and vehicle entry
tasks.detail: Getting into and out of a seat as a physical transition inside a moving frame, with the controller handing off to the vehicle.
tasks.acceptance: Board a hovering ship, take the seat and fly, with no teleport and no cut, and get out again while it is still moving.

tasks.title: Ladders, climbing and mantling
tasks.detail: Vertical movement that respects the geometry rather than snapping to it.
tasks.acceptance: Climb a ladder inside an accelerating ship and mantle onto a ledge, both with correct hand placement.

tasks.title: Carrying and manipulation animation
tasks.detail: Two-handed carry, one-handed carry, and the effect of mass on gait. Tied to M08's object handling.
tasks.acceptance: Carrying a heavy crate visibly changes stance and speed, driven by the object's mass.

tasks.title: Suits, helmets and life support on the body
tasks.detail: A person outside a breathable atmosphere needs a suit, and the suit is a component set with oxygen, temperature and pressure like any other.
tasks.acceptance: Step into vacuum without a sealed suit and die on the modelled schedule, with warnings that come from the suit's components.

tasks.title: Damage, injury and incapacitation
tasks.detail: Localised injury with effects on movement and capability, and a recovery path that is not a health bar refilling.
tasks.acceptance: A leg injury changes gait and speed until treated, and treatment consumes something.

tasks.title: Facial and upper-body animation framework
tasks.detail: Look-at, gesture, and expression driven by state rather than by canned clips, because every NPC in the living world will need it.
tasks.acceptance: A character tracks a moving object with head and eyes while walking, with no clip authored for it.

tasks.title: Character definition and variation
tasks.detail: Body proportions, faces, clothing and equipment as data, so a crowd is not twelve copies of one person.
tasks.acceptance: A hundred generated characters are visually distinct and all animate correctly on the shared rig.

tasks.title: Animation LOD and crowd cost
tasks.detail: Full evaluation up close, reduced further out, and something very cheap at distance, with transitions nobody sees.
tasks.acceptance: Two hundred visible characters stay inside the animation budget with no visible LOD switch.

tasks.title: Footstep, foley and movement audio
tasks.detail: Surface-aware footsteps, cloth, equipment, and breathing that responds to exertion and to whether there is air outside.
tasks.acceptance: Surface material is identifiable from footstep audio, and audio changes correctly in a suit and in vacuum.

tasks.title: Camera framework
tasks.detail: First person, third person, and the transitions, with collision, stabilisation and the shake budget that stops it becoming nauseating.
tasks.acceptance: Switching view is continuous, the camera never enters geometry, and motion sickness testing passes with three people.

tasks.title: Animation regression suite
tasks.detail: Recorded traversals with foot-sliding, penetration and pop metrics computed automatically, because animation regressions are invisible in a diff.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberately broken blend is caught by CI with a named metric.

tasks.title: Playable proof: room to cockpit and back
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Out of a room, up a ladder, across a pad in wind, into a ship, into a seat, fly, land, get out — one shot, no cut, nothing sliding.

tasks.title: Modular kit framework
tasks.detail: Rooms, corridors, junctions and shafts as a connectable kit with sockets, so interiors are assembled rather than modelled. The prerequisite for generated ships, stations and buildings all at once.
tasks.acceptance: An interior assembled from the kit has no gap, no z-fight at any seam, and correct collision throughout.

tasks.title: Interior generation from a layout grammar
tasks.detail: A generator that lays out an interior from a purpose and a footprint — circulation first, then rooms, then detail — rather than stamping prefabs.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty generated interiors of the same purpose are all navigable, all different, and none has an unreachable room.

tasks.title: Ship interiors on the modular kit
tasks.detail: Ship internals assembled from the same kit, constrained by the hull, with the component graph from M05 physically present in them.
tasks.acceptance: Every component in a ship's graph has a physical location inside it that can be walked to and worked on.

tasks.title: Station interiors
tasks.detail: Larger, with spin gravity, public and private volumes, docking connections and the traffic that implies.
tasks.acceptance: Walk from a docked ship into a station, across it, and into another docked ship, all in the correct frames.

tasks.title: Building interiors for settlements
tasks.detail: Habitation, industry and civic interiors, generated for the settlement layer, with the environment-driven composition from LW SS7.2 visible inside as well as outside.
tasks.acceptance: A habitat on an airless world has an airlock, a pressurised interior and visible life support; the same archetype on a temperate world does not.

tasks.title: Portals and interior streaming
tasks.detail: Interiors stream and cull through portals, so a city block of walkable buildings costs what is visible rather than what exists.
tasks.acceptance: A hundred walkable interiors in view cost no more than the handful actually visible through their openings.

tasks.title: Doors, airlocks and pressure boundaries
tasks.detail: Doors as constraints with power, pressure differential and failure. An airlock is a state machine that can kill you.
tasks.acceptance: Cycling an airlock takes time, equalises pressure, and opening the wrong door vents the compartment.

tasks.title: Interior lighting framework
tasks.detail: Lights as powered fixtures. When the district loses power, the lights go out — which is the first-person tell LW SS7.1 requires.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting power to a building darkens its interior and emergency lighting comes up on its own reserve.

tasks.title: Interior navigation mesh generation
tasks.detail: Navigation built from the assembled kit at runtime, across frames, so NPCs can move through interiors that were generated a moment ago and are themselves moving.
tasks.acceptance: A character navigates from any point in a generated interior to any other, including inside a moving ship.

tasks.title: Interior audio: reverb, occlusion, propagation
tasks.detail: Rooms sound like rooms, doors muffle, and a corridor carries sound the way a corridor does.
tasks.acceptance: Reverb and occlusion change correctly walking between three connected spaces without hand-placed volumes.

tasks.title: Set dressing and clutter framework
tasks.detail: Rule-driven placement of the objects that make a room look inhabited, responding to the room's purpose and its owner's circumstances.
tasks.acceptance: A workshop, a bunk and an office generated from the same kit are immediately distinguishable, and a wealthy one differs from a poor one.

tasks.title: Interior collision and traversal quality pass
tasks.detail: Every surface a person can reach behaves: no invisible walls, no geometry you can walk through, no ledge you catch on.
tasks.acceptance: An automated traversal agent covers every reachable point of ten generated interiors without getting stuck.

tasks.title: Playable proof: street to cockpit through a building
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Street, into a building, up through it, onto a roof pad, into a docked ship, to its cockpit — no load, no fade, no frame over budget.

tasks.title: Material standard and shading model audit
tasks.detail: One documented PBR standard: what maps, what ranges, what conventions. Half the reason a game looks amateur is materials that disagree about what roughness means.
tasks.acceptance: Every material in the project conforms, and a validator flags any that does not.

tasks.title: Master material framework with layering
tasks.detail: Layered materials with blend masks, so a hull is metal plus paint plus wear plus dirt rather than one baked texture.
tasks.acceptance: A single hull material produces a clean ship and a filthy one from parameters alone.

tasks.title: Wear, dirt and weathering framework
tasks.detail: Procedural edge wear, dirt accumulation by cavity and by exposure, driven by an object's actual history rather than authored in.
tasks.acceptance: A ship that has flown through dust looks like it, and cleaning it removes exactly that.

tasks.title: Decal framework
tasks.detail: Projected detail on hulls, terrain and interiors — markings, damage, leaks, signage — with correct normals and a budget.
tasks.acceptance: A thousand decals in view cost inside budget and none swims or z-fights.

tasks.title: Lighting: Lumen configuration and fallback
tasks.detail: Global illumination that works from a lit cockpit at night to a sunlit dune, with a measured decision about where it costs more than it gives. Design v1.1 turned it off for the slice; this is where that is revisited with numbers.
tasks.acceptance: Three reference scenes are correctly lit within budget, and the decision is recorded with measurements.

tasks.title: Shadow quality across scales
tasks.detail: Contact shadows in a cockpit, cascades across a landscape, and shadows from a moon on a planet — three problems that must share one setup.
tasks.acceptance: No shadow acne, no peter-panning and no cascade seam at any of the three scales.

tasks.title: Reflection framework
tasks.detail: Screen-space, captures and ray-traced where it pays, with a policy for what gets which. Water, canopies and polished hulls each want a different answer.
tasks.acceptance: A reflective hull, a canopy and the sea are all correct from a viewpoint that shows all three.

tasks.title: Exposure, tone mapping and colour pipeline
tasks.detail: One colour pipeline from lighting to display, handling a range from starlight to a sunlit ice field without clipping or hunting.
tasks.acceptance: Flying from a dark hangar into daylight adapts smoothly with no overshoot, and no scene clips.

tasks.title: Anti-aliasing and upscaling
tasks.detail: Temporal AA tuned against the specific problems here — thin cockpit geometry, high-frequency terrain, particles — plus an upscaler evaluated rather than assumed.
tasks.acceptance: No ghosting on cockpit instruments during rapid motion and no shimmer on terrain at any distance.

tasks.title: Particle and VFX framework
tasks.detail: Thrusters, damage, weather, dust and debris on one budgeted system, with LOD and culling and no orphaned emitters.
tasks.acceptance: Worst-case effects load stays inside budget and a two-hour session leaks no emitters.

tasks.title: Volumetric lighting and atmospherics in interiors
tasks.detail: Light shafts, dust in the air, smoke that fills a compartment — the difference between a lit room and a rendered one.
tasks.acceptance: A single window lights a dusty interior convincingly at three times of day, inside budget.

tasks.title: LOD and impostor chain for everything
tasks.detail: One policy covering ships, buildings, characters and props, with automatic generation and no visible switch.
tasks.acceptance: No LOD transition is visible at any distance for any asset class.

tasks.title: Character rendering: skin, cloth, hair, eyes
tasks.detail: The hardest thing to make not look like a mannequin, and the thing a player looks at closest.
tasks.acceptance: A character at conversation distance holds up in three lighting conditions.

tasks.title: Cockpit rendering quality pass
tasks.detail: Where the player spends most of their time: glass, displays, backlighting, reflections on the canopy, and the sun through it.
tasks.acceptance: A cockpit at dawn, at noon and at night each hold up, with legible instruments in all three.

tasks.title: Post-processing chain
tasks.detail: Bloom, motion blur, depth of field, aberration and grain, each with a reason and a budget, and each defensible against being turned off.
tasks.acceptance: Every post effect has a measured cost and a documented reason, and the chain costs no more than its budget.

tasks.title: Reference comparison harness
tasks.detail: Fixed shots against reference footage at set distances and lighting conditions, reviewed each time the renderer changes.
tasks.acceptance: The comparison set is captured automatically and archived per build.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the reference comparison
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate: side by side at three distances and three lighting conditions.
tasks.acceptance: A stranger cannot immediately sort ours from the reference on material and lighting alone.

tasks.title: Asset import and validation pipeline
tasks.detail: One path in for meshes, textures and rigs, with validation that rejects what will cause problems later — wrong scale, missing UVs, non-conforming materials, unreasonable triangle counts.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberately broken asset is rejected with a message naming the problem, not imported and discovered three weeks later.

tasks.title: Automatic LOD and collision generation
tasks.detail: LOD chains and collision proxies generated at import with per-class rules, because hand-authoring them for hundreds of assets is not a plan.
tasks.acceptance: An imported asset arrives with a full LOD chain and collision that matches its silhouette, with no manual step.

tasks.title: Material assignment and texture packing
tasks.detail: Conventions applied at import: channel packing, compression settings, streaming priorities, and material instances built from the standard.
tasks.acceptance: An imported asset renders correctly with no hand-assigned material.

tasks.title: Procedural building generator
tasks.detail: Buildings generated from purpose, footprint, environment and owner, assembling exteriors that match the interiors M10 generates.
tasks.acceptance: A generated building's exterior openings correspond exactly to its interior layout.

tasks.title: Settlement layout generator
tasks.detail: Districts, streets, utilities and pads laid out from terrain, resources and purpose, at scales from outpost to city.
tasks.acceptance: Three settlements of different scale generate on different terrain, each navigable and each explicable from its site.

tasks.title: Environment-driven building composition
tasks.detail: The LW SS7.2 rule made real in art: an archetype gains sealed envelopes, anchoring, shielding and thermal plant from the environment it is placed in.
tasks.acceptance: One archetype placed on four different worlds produces four visibly and structurally different buildings from one definition.

tasks.title: Prop and clutter library with rule-based placement
tasks.detail: The vocabulary a place is dressed from, plus the rules that place it, so a generated street is not a repeated tile.
tasks.acceptance: Two streets generated from the same rules are recognisably the same kind of place and not the same place.

tasks.title: Ship art pipeline
tasks.detail: From model to flyable: hardpoints, component locations, interior kit attachment, damage states, LODs and materials, as a repeatable process.
tasks.acceptance: A new ship goes from mesh to flyable with interiors in under a day of work.

tasks.title: Audio asset pipeline and mix framework
tasks.detail: Import conventions, buses, attenuation curves, occlusion setup and a mix that holds from a quiet interior to a storm.
tasks.acceptance: No sound clips the mix, and dialogue-range audio stays legible in the loudest scene.

tasks.title: Content authoring tools
tasks.detail: In-editor tools for defining systems, bodies, biomes, ships, buildings and settlements, so content is authored as data by a person rather than typed as code.
tasks.acceptance: A complete star system is authored end to end without editing source.

tasks.title: Content validation suite
tasks.detail: Automated checks across all content: missing references, budget violations, unreachable interiors, invalid configurations.
tasks.acceptance: Every class of content error seen during this milestone is caught automatically thereafter.

tasks.title: Asset streaming and memory budgets
tasks.detail: What is resident, what streams, at what priority, under a hard memory budget with visible accounting.
tasks.acceptance: Memory stays inside budget through a two-hour session that visits every content type.

tasks.title: Cook and package pipeline
tasks.detail: A packaged build that actually runs — including the runtime-generated materials the prototype relies on the editor for, which will not survive a cook as they stand.
tasks.acceptance: A packaged build runs the full technical slice with no editor present.

tasks.title: Playable proof: new ship and new biome end to end
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Both added through the pipeline with no manual step outside the tool, and both correct at every LOD.

tasks.title: Frame budget definition and enforcement
tasks.detail: A published budget per subsystem, instrumented, with CI failing a build that exceeds it. A budget nobody measures is a wish.
tasks.acceptance: The budget is enforced automatically and a deliberate regression fails the build.

tasks.title: Automated performance capture across scenarios
tasks.detail: Fixed scenarios — city, cockpit, orbit, storm, combat — captured every build with frame time distributions rather than averages.
tasks.acceptance: Per-build performance history is queryable and a regression is attributable to a commit.
