tasks.title: Draw call and instancing pass
tasks.detail: Batching, instancing and merging across terrain, scatter, buildings and props. The prototype's section pool alone reached thousands of components.
tasks.acceptance: Draw calls in the densest scene fall below the budget with no visual change.

tasks.title: Culling: occlusion, distance and relevance
tasks.detail: A city with interiors is mostly invisible from anywhere in it, and the renderer should know that.
tasks.acceptance: Visible triangle count in a city drops by an order of magnitude with no visible change.

tasks.title: Game thread cost reduction
tasks.detail: Tick consolidation, work distribution and removal of per-frame work that does not need to happen per frame.
tasks.acceptance: Game thread stays under its budget in the worst scenario.

tasks.title: Worker thread utilisation
tasks.detail: Terrain, physics, animation, streaming and audio across cores without contention or priority inversion.
tasks.acceptance: Core utilisation is even under load and no worker starves the game thread.

tasks.title: GPU profiling and shader cost pass
tasks.detail: Per-pass GPU cost measured and reduced, with shader complexity budgets by material class.
tasks.acceptance: Every render pass is inside its budget in the worst scenario.

tasks.title: Memory: fragmentation, leaks and long sessions
tasks.detail: Two-hour sessions with no growth, no fragmentation-driven stalls, and pools sized from measurement.
tasks.acceptance: A two-hour session ends with the memory profile it started with.

tasks.title: Load and streaming hitch elimination
tasks.detail: Every remaining stall over 4 ms hunted down. Seamlessness is destroyed by one hitch and the player remembers only the hitch.
tasks.acceptance: A full traversal of the slice shows no frame over 16 ms.

tasks.title: Scalability settings
tasks.detail: Quality levels that degrade gracefully across a range of hardware, each measured rather than assumed.
tasks.acceptance: Three quality levels are measured on three hardware profiles and each hits its target frame rate.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the density test
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Sixty frames a second with a full city, a docked ship interior and traffic in view, no frame over 16 ms, no memory growth over two hours.

tasks.title: Choose and build the slice system
tasks.detail: One star, one habitable planet, one moon, one gas giant, one asteroid field. Authored through the M12 tools, not by hand.
tasks.acceptance: The system is complete, plausible and generated reproducibly from its authored definition.

tasks.title: Build the slice city
tasks.detail: One city on the habitable planet: districts, walkable interiors, pads, utilities visible, at a scale that holds up.
tasks.acceptance: The city is walkable end to end with every building enterable and the frame budget held throughout.

tasks.title: Build the slice station
tasks.detail: One orbital station with spin gravity, docking, interiors and traffic.
tasks.acceptance: Dock, disembark, cross the station in spin gravity, and depart, all in correct frames.

tasks.title: Build the outpost on the hostile moon
tasks.detail: The environment-driven composition proof: an airless, storm-scoured site with sealed, anchored, shielded buildings and visible life support.
tasks.acceptance: The same archetypes as the city produce visibly different buildings, from environment data alone.

tasks.title: Three ships to production standard
tasks.detail: A courier, a hauler and a fighter: full component graphs, interiors, damage states, instruments and audio.
tasks.acceptance: All three are flyable, walkable, damageable and repairable, with handling differences that come from their configurations.

tasks.title: Placeholder purge
tasks.detail: Every remaining grey box, untextured mesh, programmer material and temporary sound, found and replaced or removed.
tasks.acceptance: An automated audit reports zero placeholder assets in the slice.

tasks.title: Traversal and interaction polish pass
tasks.detail: Every transition in the slice — door, ladder, seat, airlock, dock, frame change — reviewed and made to feel deliberate rather than tolerated.
tasks.acceptance: A reviewer completes every transition in the slice and reports none as rough.

tasks.title: Stability soak
tasks.detail: Long unattended and attended sessions hunting crashes, leaks, drift and state corruption.
tasks.acceptance: Ten hours of mixed play with no crash and no state corruption.

tasks.title: External playtest
tasks.detail: People who have not seen it, playing without instruction, watched. The first honest read on whether the technical model reads as a place.
tasks.acceptance: Five testers complete a free-play session and their observations are recorded and triaged.

tasks.title: Technical slice review and ADR
tasks.detail: What the model proved, what it did not, and what the simulation layer must now be built against. The decision point the whole technical plan exists to inform.
tasks.acceptance: An ADR recording what was proven and any changes it forces on the simulation plan.

tasks.title: Playable proof: an hour of free play
tasks.detail: Rule 6, and the milestone gate. This is the moment the project either has a technical foundation or does not.
tasks.acceptance: An hour of unscripted play with no loading screen, no crash, no frame over 16 ms, and nothing that reads as placeholder.

tasks.title: Event type registry with stable wire ids
tasks.detail: Events are the log format and the log outlives every refactor. Each event gets an id that never changes and a version.
tasks.acceptance: Renaming an event struct does not change its id, and a test proves it.

tasks.title: Reducer contract and per-crate registration
tasks.detail: Each domain crate contributes reducers over its own slice of state; ledger-world composes them without knowing what they do.
tasks.acceptance: Adding a crate's reducer requires no edit to ledger-world beyond one registration line.

tasks.title: Snapshot format with content hashing
tasks.detail: A snapshot is bytes plus a hash of those bytes, so divergence is detected rather than described.
tasks.acceptance: Two runs from one seed produce identical hashes and a one-bit change is detected.

tasks.title: Replay from snapshot plus tail
tasks.detail: Load a snapshot, apply subsequent events, and arrive where a full replay from zero arrives.
tasks.acceptance: Snapshot-plus-tail and full replay agree byte for byte at 100,000 ticks.

tasks.title: Determinism harness in CI
tasks.detail: Run the same scenario twice in separate processes and diff. Cross-platform where CI allows, because that is where float creep hides.
tasks.acceptance: CI fails on divergence and names the first differing tick.

tasks.title: Static check: no floating point in authoritative state
tasks.detail: A test that walks the type graph of State and rejects f32 and f64.
tasks.acceptance: Introducing a float into any authoritative struct fails a test.

tasks.title: Tick scheduler with fixed step and bounded catch-up
tasks.detail: Simulation time advances in fixed steps regardless of wall clock, with catch-up bounded so a slow frame cannot spiral.
tasks.acceptance: Stalling the process for ten seconds leaves the sim consistent rather than ahead of itself.

tasks.title: Command intake as the only entry point
tasks.detail: External intent becomes a validated command, which becomes events. No system mutates state directly.
tasks.acceptance: A test proves no reducer is reachable except through a command.

tasks.title: Scenario definition format
tasks.detail: A seed, an initial state and a script of commands. Every acceptance test from here to the end of the roadmap is written as one.
tasks.acceptance: A scenario file runs headless and produces a stable dump.

tasks.title: Event log persistence and compaction
tasks.detail: Write the log, read it back, and compact old regions behind snapshots so it does not grow without bound.
tasks.acceptance: A one-year log compacts and still replays to the same hash.

tasks.title: Event schema migration
tasks.detail: Old logs must replay after the schema moves. Versioned events with upgrade functions.
tasks.acceptance: A log written against version 1 replays under version 2.

tasks.title: Causal trace: why did this happen
tasks.detail: Every event carries its cause, so tracing a collapse back four causes becomes a property of the log rather than of one printer.
tasks.acceptance: Any event walks back to a root cause with no domain-specific code.

tasks.title: Sim-to-client wire contract
tasks.detail: The snapshot and command formats the client's bridge module speaks, versioned, with a recorded stream to test against.
tasks.acceptance: A recorded stream replays into the client and produces the same world.

tasks.title: Per-crate tick budget and profiling
tasks.detail: Where the tick goes, per crate, so the answer at M23 is measured rather than guessed.
tasks.acceptance: A run prints tick cost by crate and flags any crate over budget.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the client renders a replayed world
tasks.detail: Rule 6. Feed the client a snapshot stream from a replayed log rather than a live sim and confirm the boundary is honest.
tasks.acceptance: The client renders identically from a live sim and from a replay of it.

tasks.title: Agent identity, attributes and lifecycle
tasks.detail: Who someone is, what they are capable of, and how they enter and leave the world. Birth, hiring, death and disappearance are all lifecycle events.
tasks.acceptance: Ten thousand agents are created, tracked and retired over a simulated year with no leak and no orphan.

tasks.title: Needs and drives
tasks.detail: Income, safety, standing, belonging, grudge — the pressures that make an agent want anything. Needs decay and are satisfied; they are not a mood.
tasks.acceptance: An agent deprived of income changes behaviour in a way traceable to the need, and satisfying it changes behaviour back.

tasks.title: Goal representation and prioritisation
tasks.detail: A goal is a desired world state with a weight. Agents hold several and reprioritise as needs and beliefs change.
tasks.acceptance: An agent's goal set is inspectable and its ordering is explained by its needs.

tasks.title: Planner over world state
tasks.detail: From a goal and a set of available actions, produce a plan. Hierarchical and interruptible, because plans in this world get invalidated constantly.
tasks.acceptance: An agent plans a multi-step route to a goal, is interrupted, and replans without restarting from nothing.

tasks.title: Agents plan against beliefs, not world state
tasks.detail: The single most important property in the framework. A planner that reads world state is a planner that is omniscient, and an omniscient agent cannot be deceived, which destroys the entire information design.
tasks.acceptance: A test proves the planner cannot reach world state, and an agent with a false belief plans as though it were true.

tasks.title: Perception and belief formation
tasks.detail: Agents observe what they can see, are told what others tell them, and form beliefs with provenance and confidence. The existing belief graph gets its producers.
tasks.acceptance: An agent that witnesses an event believes it firsthand; one told about it believes it at a lower confidence with a named source.

tasks.title: Action library and execution
tasks.detail: The vocabulary of what an agent can do — move, work, trade, talk, fight, wait — with preconditions, effects, duration and cost. Data, not a switch statement.
tasks.acceptance: Adding an action is one definition and the planner uses it with no other change.

tasks.title: Schedules and routine
tasks.detail: Agents have lives: work, rest, travel, obligations. Routine is what makes a world look inhabited rather than idle.
tasks.acceptance: A day in an agent's life is legible from a trace and repeats with variation rather than exactly.

tasks.title: Competence and failure
tasks.detail: Agents differ in skill and fail at things. A plan that assumed success and got failure must be recoverable from.
tasks.acceptance: Two agents with different competence attempting the same action produce measurably different outcome distributions.

tasks.title: Loyalty, relationships and social graph
tasks.detail: Who an agent trusts, owes, resents and reports to — the substrate for delegation, betrayal and bribery, which are all one system.
tasks.acceptance: An agent's willingness to act against another is computed from the relationship graph, not stored as a flag.

tasks.title: Communication: agents telling each other things
tasks.detail: Conversation as belief transfer with latency, selection and distortion. Agents choose what to share based on who they are talking to.
tasks.acceptance: A fact crosses a social network with the decay, hop count and distortion the belief model specifies.

tasks.title: Deception: agents that lie
tasks.detail: An agent can assert something it does not believe, with a motive derived from its goals. The receiver has no way to know except through provenance and corroboration.
tasks.acceptance: An agent with a motive to deceive does, and the false belief propagates and is later contradicted by a firsthand observation.

tasks.title: Agent scale: level of detail for simulation
tasks.detail: Fifty thousand agents cannot all plan every tick. Full simulation near the player, statistical further out, with promotion and demotion that does not lose state or produce a visible discontinuity.
tasks.acceptance: An agent demoted to statistical and later promoted has a history consistent with what it would have done, and the transition is invisible.

tasks.title: Agent debugging and inspection tools
tasks.detail: Pick any agent and see its needs, goals, plan, beliefs, relationships and the reasoning behind its current action. Without this the framework is unmaintainable.
tasks.acceptance: Any agent's current action is explained in one screen with no code reading.

tasks.title: Agent behaviour regression suite
tasks.detail: Scenarios asserting agents respond correctly to needs, beliefs, deception and failure, so a change to the planner is caught rather than discovered.
tasks.acceptance: Each property in this milestone has a scenario that fails when broken.

tasks.title: Client integration: agents as embodied characters
tasks.detail: Agents drive the characters M09 built, through the entity-view framework. A sim agent walking to work is a person walking down a street.
tasks.acceptance: Two hundred simulated agents are visible as characters going about traceable business, inside the frame budget.

tasks.title: Playable proof: 500 agents for 30 days
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Any agent's whole history is explained by its needs and beliefs with no appeal to world state it never observed, and two agents with different beliefs act differently.

tasks.title: Organisation entity and charter
tasks.detail: Charter, members, holdings, fleet, treasury, doctrine. One type, used by player and NPC organisations alike — ARCH Rule 4 is enforced here or nowhere.
tasks.acceptance: A test asserts no branch in the org crate reads a player flag.

tasks.title: Membership, roles and authority
tasks.detail: Who belongs, in what role, with what authority to commit the organisation's resources.
tasks.acceptance: An action exceeding a member's authority is refused, and the refusal is visible to the member who attempted it.

tasks.title: Doctrine as goal weighting
tasks.detail: Doctrine weights goal generation so a mercantile organisation answers a supply problem with a contract and a predatory one with a raid. Flavour text that does not change behaviour is not doctrine.
tasks.acceptance: Two organisations with identical assets and different doctrine produce measurably different action distributions.

tasks.title: Treasury, budgets and financial state
tasks.detail: Income, expenditure, reserves and the ability to commit to something that has not been paid for yet.
tasks.acceptance: An organisation cannot spend what it does not have, and insolvency has consequences that propagate to its members.

tasks.title: Holdings and asset ownership
tasks.detail: Stations, claims, facilities, ships — what an organisation owns, what it earns from them, and what it is exposed to by them.
tasks.acceptance: Transferring a holding moves income and vulnerability together, with the change propagating through the belief graph rather than instantly.

tasks.title: Span of control and oversight
tasks.detail: Oversight demand from assets against supply from members, with the deficit expressed as drift rather than as a number.
tasks.acceptance: Oversight demand and supply are computable and their ratio predicts the drift rate observed in a scenario.

tasks.title: Drift: subordinates acting on their own goals
tasks.detail: The consequence of the deficit, expressed entirely through the agent framework. Unauthorised routes, skimming, late execution, private agendas — all agents pursuing their own goals because nobody is watching.
tasks.acceptance: Drift emerges from agent goals with no code in the org layer that produces it directly.

tasks.title: Founding an organisation
tasks.detail: Capital, a public charter, and registration with an existing authority — which means an authority now has an opinion about you.
tasks.acceptance: A player organisation is founded through the same API an NPC one is, and the chartering authority's disposition changes as a result.

tasks.title: Organisation-level goals and decision making
tasks.detail: Organisations want things: growth, security, revenue, revenge. Goals generated from state and doctrine, decomposed into directives for members.
tasks.acceptance: An organisation's current goals are inspectable and each traces to a state fact and a doctrine weight.

tasks.title: Hiring, firing and defection
tasks.detail: Members join and leave for reasons in their own goal systems. An underpaid, unwatched or resentful subordinate is a recruitable one.
tasks.acceptance: An agent defects to a rival when the rival's offer beats their current position on their own terms, and the org learns of it late.

tasks.title: Standing as belief, not as a number
tasks.detail: Organisations do not own reputations. Other organisations hold beliefs about them, and those beliefs disagree.
tasks.acceptance: A test asserts no reputation field exists, and two organisations demonstrably hold different beliefs about a third.

tasks.title: Organisation inspection tools
tasks.detail: Membership, holdings, finances, goals, drift and standing for any organisation, plus the reasoning behind its current decisions.
tasks.acceptance: Any organisation's current behaviour is explicable from one screen.

tasks.title: Organisation regression suite
tasks.detail: Scenarios for drift, defection, insolvency, doctrine divergence and founding.
tasks.acceptance: Each property has a scenario that fails when broken.

tasks.title: Playable proof: over-extend an organisation
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Drift appears as subordinates pursuing their own goals, with no code path in the org layer asking whether the owner is a player.

tasks.title: Goods, commodities and material properties
tasks.detail: What exists, what it weighs, what it takes up, what it is worth and what it is made from. The vocabulary production and construction are written in.
tasks.acceptance: The goods table is data, and adding a commodity requires no code.

tasks.title: Production chains
tasks.detail: Facilities that consume inputs and produce outputs at a rate, with the labour and power they need. Ore becomes metal becomes components becomes ships.
tasks.acceptance: A chain three deep runs for a simulated year with conservation holding at every stage.

tasks.title: Local markets with real price formation
tasks.detail: Prices from local supply, local demand and what traders believe about elsewhere — not a global price table with noise.
tasks.acceptance: Two markets in one system hold different prices for the same good, and the difference is explained by supply and by transport cost.

tasks.title: Conservation invariants
tasks.detail: Goods and money are conserved except at explicit mint and sink events. The prototype proved this at small scale; it must hold at large scale.
tasks.acceptance: A simulated year across thirty-two systems conserves both to the unit.

tasks.title: Contracts and obligations
tasks.detail: Agreements to deliver, to pay, to protect, with terms, deadlines and penalties, resting on the existing obligation ledger.
tasks.acceptance: A breached contract has consequences that propagate as belief and as obligation, not as a number changing.

tasks.title: Transport and convoys
tasks.detail: Goods move physically, take time, and can be intercepted. This is what makes distance strategic and a convoy a target.
tasks.acceptance: A shipment's arrival time matches the route's travel time, and destroying it removes the goods from the destination's supply.

tasks.title: Supply shock propagation
tasks.detail: A disruption in one place moves through markets at the speed of transport and information, not instantly.
tasks.acceptance: A shock moves prices three systems away with a lag matching travel time, and the lag is measurable.

tasks.title: Labour markets
tasks.detail: Agents want work, organisations want workers, and wages come from that meeting. Underpaying is possible and has consequences.
tasks.acceptance: A labour shortage raises wages, and an organisation that will not pay loses workers to one that will.

tasks.title: Currency, credit and debt
tasks.detail: Money that is issued somewhere, credit that can be extended and defaulted on, and debt as a relationship rather than a number.
tasks.acceptance: A default damages the creditor's position and the debtor's standing, both through existing systems.

tasks.title: Economic inspection and dashboards
tasks.detail: Prices, flows, shortages, production and trade routes, inspectable across the whole simulation.
tasks.acceptance: A shortage anywhere is visible in the dashboard and traceable to its cause.

tasks.title: Economic balance and anti-degeneracy
tasks.detail: Long runs looking for the failure modes: hyperinflation, dead markets, monopoly, infinite loops. Each found and given a mechanism that resists it.
tasks.acceptance: Ten one-year runs from different seeds end with functioning economies and no runaway.

tasks.title: Economy regression suite
tasks.detail: Conservation, price formation, shock propagation and contract enforcement as scenarios.
tasks.acceptance: Each property has a scenario that fails when broken.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the supply shock
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: A shock moves prices three systems away with the right lag; ninety days with no negative inventory and no money created outside a mint.

tasks.title: Site and environment profile
tasks.detail: Atmosphere, pressure, temperature, weather, gravity and local resources as the data a site is defined by — read from the physical fields M04 already computes rather than authored separately.
tasks.acceptance: A site's environment matches what the renderer and the weather model say at that location, always.

tasks.title: Claims and registration
tasks.detail: Claiming land is registering with an authority, which creates a relationship. Claims far from authority are cheap and unprotected.
tasks.acceptance: A claim registered with an authority changes that authority's disposition; an unregistered one is defensible only by force.

tasks.title: Structure archetypes and module derivation
tasks.detail: A building is an archetype plus the modules its environment demands. The rule from LW SS7.2 as code: sealed envelope, anchoring, shielding, thermal plant, each derived rather than chosen.
tasks.acceptance: One archetype on four environments produces four different structures with different capital cost, power load and maintenance rate.

tasks.title: Utility network model: power
tasks.detail: Generation, distribution and consumption as a graph with capacity and throughput. The network everything else depends on.
tasks.acceptance: Demand exceeding supply sheds load in priority order, and the shortfall is attributable to a node or an edge.

tasks.title: Utility networks: life support, water, transit
tasks.detail: The other three, on the same graph machinery. Life support exists only where the environment demands it, which is why some cities are fragile.
tasks.acceptance: All four networks run on one implementation, and a city on a breathable world has three of them.

tasks.title: Cascade failure
tasks.detail: Lose power, lose life support, lose the district. One directed cascade, and it is enough for all of city crisis modelling.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting a power node causes exactly the downstream failures the graph predicts, in the order it predicts.

tasks.title: Construction projects as directives
tasks.detail: A project has a site, a design, materials that must physically arrive, labour that must be present, and a schedule that weather and people can disrupt.
tasks.acceptance: A project on a remote world is delayed by a late convoy and by a storm, and both delays are traceable.

tasks.title: Construction as a visible process
tasks.detail: Foundations, scaffolding, partial structures and crews. A building under construction is a place, not a progress bar.
tasks.acceptance: A project is identifiable by sight at four stages of completion.

tasks.title: Structure condition and degradation
tasks.detail: Everything wears, faster in hostile environments, and the wear is visible before it is fatal.
tasks.acceptance: Degradation rate tracks the environment, and a neglected structure is visibly neglected before it fails.

tasks.title: Work orders and maintenance crews
tasks.detail: Degradation produces work orders; crews are agents with the maintain goal, their own competence, and their own beliefs about which conduit is broken.
tasks.acceptance: A crew fed a false belief about a fault location goes to the wrong district, and the right one stays dark.

tasks.title: Unhandled work becomes contracts
tasks.detail: What an organisation cannot staff goes on the open board. This is where a new player finds their first job, long before they know there is a strategic layer generating it.
tasks.acceptance: An understaffed organisation's backlog appears as public contracts, and taking one clears the work order.

tasks.title: District state and population
tasks.detail: Who lives and works where, what they need, and what happens when the district cannot provide it — including leaving.
tasks.acceptance: A district that loses life support evacuates, and the population appears somewhere else rather than vanishing.

tasks.title: City growth and decline
tasks.detail: Settlements grow where there is reason and shrink where there is not, driven by the economy rather than by a curve.
tasks.acceptance: A city grows a district in response to sustained economic demand and abandons one when the demand goes.

tasks.title: The six first-person tells
tasks.detail: LW SS7.1, implemented and verified: dark districts, masks indoors, shutters in a storm, deferred maintenance, contested markers, scaffolding. A mechanic without a tell does not ship.
tasks.acceptance: All six are observable by walking through a running city, and each is driven by the simulation rather than triggered for display.

tasks.title: Utilities as military targets
tasks.detail: A holding whose power fails is a holding that dies, which makes utilities worth attacking and worth defending.
tasks.acceptance: Destroying a generator has the strategic effect the cascade model implies, and the owner responds.

tasks.title: Settlement inspection tools
tasks.detail: Networks, loads, conditions, work orders, population and projects, inspectable for any settlement.
tasks.acceptance: Any settlement failure is diagnosable from the tools without reading code.

tasks.title: Playable proof: cut the power to a district
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Life support fails, crews respond, people put masks on, and the district evacuates — all visible from the street.

tasks.title: Believed power estimation
tasks.detail: What an organisation thinks another is worth fearing, assembled from beliefs about fleet, holdings, income and allies — every one of them capable of being wrong.
tasks.acceptance: Two organisations hold different estimates of a third, and each estimate is explained by what that observer has actually heard.

tasks.title: Threat model and alarm
tasks.detail: Alarm from believed power, proximity, dependency, rivalry history and the observer's own strength. The formula in LW SS3.1, and it reads belief rather than truth.
tasks.acceptance: A test proves the threat model cannot reach ground truth, and alarm responds correctly to each of its five inputs in isolation.

tasks.title: Dependency: you do not attack your supplier
tasks.detail: Economic dependency suppresses alarm, which makes being useful a genuine alternative to being feared — and a different way to play.
tasks.acceptance: Establishing a supply relationship measurably lowers the customer's alarm, and severing it raises it again.

tasks.title: Coalition formation
tasks.detail: When several organisations independently cross alarm about the same subject and are not blocked by mutual hostility, they discover each other. The pact is a coincidence of alarm, not a script.
tasks.acceptance: A coalition forms in a scenario with no code that decides a coalition should form, and its members can each state why they joined.

tasks.title: Coalition instability and dissolution
tasks.detail: Every member runs the threat model on every other member. A coalition dissolves when the target falls below threshold or a partner rises above one.
tasks.acceptance: A coalition dissolves for both reasons in separate scenarios.

tasks.title: Counterplay: hiding, bribing, fracturing, being useful
tasks.detail: The four strategies in LW SS3.1, each of which must actually work: suppress information, redirect a member's alarm, feed one member a belief about another, or become indispensable.
tasks.acceptance: Each of the four demonstrably breaks or prevents a coalition in a scenario.

tasks.title: Visibility: the informational ceiling
tasks.detail: Assets generate observable events. The larger an organisation, the more surface it presents and the harder believed power is to suppress.
tasks.acceptance: Observable event rate scales with organisation size, and a large organisation cannot reach the concealment a small one can.

tasks.title: Legitimacy: the economic ceiling
tasks.detail: A holding taken by force needs a garrison forever; one taken by contract needs an accountant. Two cost curves that cross.
tasks.acceptance: Coercive and commercial acquisition of the same holding have costs whose curves cross at a computable point.

tasks.title: Hostility, war and peace states
tasks.detail: Relationships between organisations as states with entry and exit conditions, driven by alarm and by events rather than declared.
tasks.acceptance: A war starts from a traceable sequence of events and ends when the conditions that sustained it stop holding.

tasks.title: Intelligence operations
tasks.detail: Deliberately acquiring and denying information: agents placed, sources cultivated, feeds poisoned. The belief system's offensive use.
tasks.acceptance: An intelligence operation measurably changes a rival's threat model, and can be detected and countered.

tasks.title: Power inspection tools
tasks.detail: Every organisation's threat model, alarm levels, coalitions and their reasons, inspectable and explicable.
tasks.acceptance: Any coalition's formation is explained from the tools without reading code.

tasks.title: Power balance testing
tasks.detail: Long runs looking for runaway victory and for stagnation. The ceiling is supposed to be a plateau, not a wall and not a cliff.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty one-year runs produce neither a runaway hegemon nor a frozen balance.

tasks.title: Playable proof: provoke a coalition, then fracture it
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Rivals independently cross alarm and coordinate; a fabricated belief fed to one member then breaks the pact.

tasks.title: Tension detection
tasks.detail: Scan the world for someone who believes something, wants something, and lacks the means. Everything a mission can be starts here.
tasks.acceptance: Tension detection returns results in a running world, and each names the parties, the belief and the shortfall.

tasks.title: Mission grammar
tasks.detail: Turning a tension into something a person could be paid to do: goal, constraints, stake, deadline, payer. A grammar, not a template list.
tasks.acceptance: Every generated mission traces to a specific tension, and removing the tension removes the mission.

tasks.title: Stakes: nothing is generated that does not matter
tasks.detail: Every mission changes the world on success or failure. A mission whose stake is only money should not have been emitted.
tasks.acceptance: A test rejects any mission whose only stake is a payment, and every generated mission's stake is a state change.

tasks.title: Offer selection: who would offer this to you
tasks.detail: A mission is offered based on what the offering party believes about the recipient. Nobody hires an unknown for a decapitation.
tasks.acceptance: The same tension produces different offers to agents of different standing, and no offer exceeds what the offerer believes the recipient capable of.

tasks.title: Mission resolution and consequence
tasks.detail: Success, failure and partial outcomes feeding back as events, beliefs and obligations. The consequence is the point.
tasks.acceptance: Completing a mission changes the world in the way its stake stated, and the change propagates as belief rather than as fact.

tasks.title: Directive representation
tasks.detail: Intent, assets, constraints and a delegate. A standing order the simulation resolves whether or not anyone is watching.
tasks.acceptance: A directive is issued, persists across a save, and continues resolving.

tasks.title: Directive resolution through agents
tasks.detail: A directive is executed by the delegate's own planner, on the delegate's own beliefs, with their competence and their interests. This is where drift comes from and it is not a separate system.
tasks.acceptance: A directive given to an incompetent or disloyal delegate produces a different outcome than the same directive to a good one, with the difference explained by the agent.

tasks.title: The presence dividend
tasks.detail: Doing something yourself is better in kind, not by a percentage: current information, the ability to change your mind, nobody skimming, and morale.
tasks.acceptance: The same task executed personally and by directive differ in all four stated ways, each measurable.

tasks.title: Player directives become other people's missions
tasks.detail: At the top you generate the tension. A directive that moves a fleet creates the shortfall a courier is hired against, through the same generator.
tasks.acceptance: A player directive produces a mission on the open board for an NPC, with no special code path.

tasks.title: Contract board and mission presentation
tasks.detail: How offers reach a player: boards, brokers, direct approach, and rumour. What is visible depends on where you are and who trusts you.
tasks.acceptance: Two players in different places with different standing see different boards, and the difference is explained by belief.

tasks.title: Mission inspection tools
tasks.detail: Every generated mission with its tension, parties, stake and reasoning, plus what happened to the ones nobody took.
tasks.acceptance: Any mission on any board is explicable from the tools.

tasks.title: Mission quality and variety testing
tasks.detail: Long runs checking that generated missions are varied, that stakes matter, and that no degenerate pattern dominates.
tasks.acceptance: A one-year run produces missions across all tension classes with no single pattern exceeding a stated share.

tasks.title: Playable proof: a directive left alone for a week
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: It resolves through subordinates, correctly or otherwise, and the outcome is explained by the delegate's beliefs and competence.

tasks.title: Command lens framework
tasks.detail: A lens over the simulation, not a mode. It does not pause the world and it does not move your body — which is still standing wherever you left it.
tasks.acceptance: Opening Command mid-flight leaves the ship flying and the world running, and closing it returns to an unchanged cockpit.

tasks.title: The map is built from reports, not ground truth
tasks.detail: Everything displayed is something somebody reported. A Command lens showing truth would destroy the entire information design.
tasks.acceptance: A test proves the Command data path cannot reach world state, and an unobserved fact does not appear on the map.

tasks.title: Staleness and confidence in the interface
tasks.detail: A three-day-old report looks three days old. Confidence, provenance and hop count are visible rather than flattened into a number.
tasks.acceptance: A stale report is visibly stale and its source is inspectable.

tasks.title: Issuing directives from Command
tasks.detail: Select assets, choose intent, set constraints, assign a delegate. The UI over M21's directive system.
tasks.acceptance: Every directive type is issuable from Command and resolves identically to one issued programmatically.

tasks.title: Reports and the intelligence view
tasks.detail: What your people have told you, when, and how much you should believe it — including reports that contradict each other.
tasks.acceptance: Two contradictory reports are both shown with their sources rather than one silently winning.

tasks.title: Organisation management screens
tasks.detail: Members, roles, finances, holdings, doctrine and the oversight deficit — the last of which is where a player learns what drift is.
tasks.acceptance: An over-extended organisation shows the deficit and the player can act on it before drift becomes damage.

tasks.title: Scale transitions in the interface
tasks.detail: From a district to a system to the region, without a load and without losing context.
tasks.acceptance: Zooming from a street to a region is continuous and never loses the selected entity.

tasks.title: Your body while you are in Command
tasks.detail: You are still standing somewhere, and someone might be looking for you. The tension that stops Command being a safe menu.
tasks.acceptance: A hostile agent can find and act on the player's body while Command is open.

tasks.title: Notifications and interruption
tasks.detail: What is worth telling the player, when, and how not to bury it. An organisation with four hundred problems generates four hundred events.
tasks.acceptance: A hundred simultaneous events produce a legible summary rather than a hundred notifications.

tasks.title: Playable proof: Command mid-flight
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: The world does not pause, the ship does not stop, a stale report is visibly stale, and an unobserved fact is absent.

tasks.title: Combat resolution shared across scales
tasks.detail: Personal, ship and asset-scale violence through one model, so a raid resolves the same way whether the player fights it or reads about it.
tasks.acceptance: The same engagement fought in person and resolved in Command produces outcomes from one distribution.

tasks.title: Bodyguards, escorts and security
tasks.detail: The things that happen to people who become worth attacking, expressed as agents with the protect goal rather than as a stat.
tasks.acceptance: A bodyguard interposes because its planner decided to, and can fail, be bribed, or be elsewhere.

tasks.title: Raids and invasions
tasks.detail: Organisation-scale operations against holdings, resolved through directives and agents, with the utility-network consequences from M19.
tasks.acceptance: A raid on a holding takes it, damages it, or fails, and the outcome propagates through ownership, belief and the economy.

tasks.title: Cross-system integration pass
tasks.detail: Every framework wired to every other one it should touch, and the seams found by running rather than by reading.
tasks.acceptance: A one-month run exercises every framework and every interaction between them without an error.

tasks.title: Long-run stability: one simulated year
tasks.detail: The test the whole simulation plan is aimed at. Runaways, deadlocks, drift to zero, and agents stuck in loops all show up here and nowhere earlier.
tasks.acceptance: A simulated year completes unattended with no crash, no deadlock and no unbounded quantity.

tasks.title: Emergence review and tuning
tasks.detail: Read a year of world history and ask whether it is interesting. Tune the mechanisms rather than adding new ones — that discipline is what stops the system becoming unexplainable.
tasks.acceptance: A year's history is readable as a story with causes, and every adjustment made is to a parameter with a stated meaning.

tasks.title: Simulation performance at scale
tasks.detail: Fifty thousand agents across thirty-two systems inside the tick budget, with the level-of-detail system from M16 carrying the load.
tasks.acceptance: The tick budget holds at target scale, with cost attributable per crate.

tasks.title: Save, load and persistence at scale
tasks.detail: A world with a year of history saves and loads without losing state and without taking minutes.
tasks.acceptance: A one-year world round-trips in under thirty seconds with a matching hash.

tasks.title: Failure and recovery
tasks.detail: What happens when the simulation stalls, diverges or crashes, with the client degrading honestly rather than inventing state.
tasks.acceptance: Killing the simulation mid-session degrades the client visibly and recovers on restart with no invented facts.

tasks.title: World dump at full scale
tasks.detail: The SS12 dump, still legible with a year of history and thirty-two systems in it. If it is not legible, the world is not understandable.
tasks.acceptance: A collapse anywhere in a year-old world is traceable back four causes from the dump.

tasks.title: Playable proof: a year, unattended
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: No runaway monopoly, no dead economy, no organisation with a thousand ships, no agent stuck in a loop, and a dump that still explains itself.

tasks.title: Arrival: the opening
tasks.detail: A player with nothing, in a place, with something to do within a minute. No cutscene, no tutorial, no character creation wall.
tasks.acceptance: A new player has a reason to move within sixty seconds of gaining control.

tasks.title: The early loop: work, information, a little money
tasks.detail: Cargo, messages, and what you learn on the way — the design's premise made playable at the smallest scale.
tasks.acceptance: A player can earn a living from generated work alone for three sessions without repetition becoming visible.

tasks.title: Building a crew
tasks.detail: Hiring the first people, who are agents with their own goals and can leave, and learning what delegation costs.
tasks.acceptance: A hired agent executes work independently, and does it badly if hired badly.

tasks.title: Founding the organisation
tasks.detail: Capital, charter and registration, and the relationship with the chartering authority that comes with it.
tasks.acceptance: A player founds an organisation and the chartering authority's disposition changes measurably as a result.

tasks.title: First holding: claim, build, maintain
tasks.detail: Claim ground, build on it, and discover that it needs power, people and attention.
tasks.acceptance: A player builds a holding, has it degrade through neglect, and repairs it, all through the M19 systems.

tasks.title: Being noticed
tasks.detail: The point at which rivals form beliefs about you and act on them — the first time the world pushes back.
tasks.acceptance: A growing player organisation becomes the subject of a rival's threat model, and the player can see evidence of it before it acts.

tasks.title: The Command transition
tasks.detail: Not a mode unlock: the Command lens goes from empty to necessary because the player owns too much to be everywhere.
tasks.acceptance: Playtesters reach the point of using Command without being told to, because presence alone stopped being sufficient.

tasks.title: The coalition
tasks.detail: The end of the arc: several organisations independently conclude the player is the problem and discover each other.
tasks.acceptance: A coalition forms against a player organisation in ordinary play, and the player can see why from Command.

tasks.title: Counterplay made discoverable
tasks.detail: Hide, bribe, fracture, be useful — all four available and all four findable without a tutorial explaining them.
tasks.acceptance: Playtesters find at least two of the four unprompted.

tasks.title: Onboarding without a tutorial
tasks.detail: The systems teach themselves through consequence and through the interface, because a tutorial for this design would be an hour long.
tasks.acceptance: A new player reaches the organisation stage with no explicit tutorial and can state the rules they learned.

tasks.title: Full playtest cycle
tasks.detail: External testers through the whole arc, watched, with findings triaged and acted on.
tasks.acceptance: Ten testers complete the arc; their findings are recorded, triaged and either fixed or explicitly deferred.

tasks.title: Balance pass across the whole arc
tasks.detail: Pacing from nothing to coalition: too fast is meaningless, too slow is a second job.
tasks.acceptance: Median time to the coalition falls inside the intended band across ten playtests.

tasks.title: Final stability and polish
tasks.detail: Crashes, corruption, soft locks, and every rough edge testers named.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty hours of mixed play with no crash, no corruption and no soft lock.

tasks.title: Playable proof: nothing to coalition, one save
tasks.detail: Rule 6, and the end of the roadmap as written. Everything since M00 exists to make this sentence true.
tasks.acceptance: A player who has never seen the game goes from nothing to a chartered organisation to a coalition forming against them, in one save, with no tutorial explaining any of the systems.
